utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Madam Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, would you please call the case which is on the Appeals Chamber's agenda of the International Tribunal today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-97-25-A, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I want to make sure that the interpreters are here and that they can hear me. Yes, they do. The accused is in the courtroom. First of all I would like to ask for the appearances of the parties. Turning first to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour, may it please the Chamber, my name is Christopher Staker. I appear today on behalf of the Prosecution with my colleagues Mr. Anthony Carmona, Miss Norul Rashid, and Miss Helen Brady. Our case manager today is Ms. Nicola Bonfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let me turn to the Defence. Could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, and my colleague Miroslav Vasic is with me to represent the accused Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We can then proceed. First of all, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to make an introductory remark for this hearing which will explain how first of all we're going to do this morning and what our organisation will be for the hearing. There seems to be no room here. All right. The Appeals Chamber is holdings its appeals hearing today in the case the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac. On the 12th of April 2002, Milorad Krnojelac appealed against the judgement of Trial Chamber II of this Tribunal on the 15th of March, 2002. The Trial Chamber, let me remind you, found Mr. Krnojelac guilty first of all pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute because of his individual responsibility as an aider and abettor of the following crimes: Charge 1 of the indictment, persecutions, crime against humanity, because of imprisonment and inhumane acts related to living conditions. Count 15 of the indictment, cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war because of the living conditions. In addition, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute, the accused was also found guilty as a superior officer of the following crimes: Ground 1 -- charge -- Count 1 of the indictment, persecutions, a crime against humanity, cruel treatment; Count 5 of the indictment, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity because of cruel treatment; and Count 7 of the indictment, cruel treatment, a violations of the laws or customs of war because of cruel treatment. Let me remind you that the Trial Chamber sentenced Milorad Krnojelac to a single sentence of 7 and a half years. On the 15th of April, 2002, the Prosecutor also appealed against that judgement. Before hearing the parties's arguments, the Appeals Chamber will recall the list of grounds of appeal which were presented by both Mr. Krnojelac and by the Prosecutor. As regards the appeal by Mr. Krnojelac, the Appeals Chamber has brought the -- regrouped the grounds of appeal in the following way. I call your attention to that. First ground: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed errors of fact in evaluating its position of prison warden which was the post that Milorad Krnojelac occupied. Let me slow down a little bit. I think I'm speaking too fast for the interpreters. And this ground has several sections. The first is that the Trial Chamber committed an error by asserting that the functions or the powers of the prison warden had barely changed after the outbreak of the armed conflict. Second ground - this is still the first ground of appeal - the Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error by asserting that Krnojelac freely had accepted the position of prison warden. Third ground: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error by asserting that Krnojelac had authority over the entire staff and detainees of the KP Dom. Fourth: The Trial Chamber did not properly evaluate the statements of witnesses that were not Serbs. Those are statements of the Prosecution. That is the first ground of appeal of Mr. Krnojelac. Second ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of law by asserting that Krnojelac had become an aider and abettor in persecution because of imprisonment and living conditions. Third ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of fact by concluding that Krnojelac had made himself guilty -- an aider and abettor in cruel treatment because of the living conditions. Fourth ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of fact by stating that Krnojelac had as a superior was -- had responsibility for the persecutions which had been caused by cruel treatment. The fifth ground is that the Appeals Chamber -- the Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of fact by stating that Krnojelac as a superior was responsible for the inhumane acts and cruel treatment under torture. As regards of the Prosecution's appeal, the Prosecution put forward seven. The first -- that is, the Chamber put them into seven groups. The first is that the Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of law in its definition of responsibility stemming from participation in a joint criminal enterprise and in the application of that definition to the facts of the case. Second ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of law by requiring that the indictment take note of a broadened form of the joint criminal enterprise. Third ground: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of fact by concluding that Krnojelac did not know and did not have reason to know that his subordinates were torturing detainees and by considering therefore that could not be held responsible under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Fourth ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of fact by concluding under Article 7(3) of the Statute that the information which Krnojelac had were not sufficient to warn his subordinates that they -- or warn him that his subordinates were implicated in the murder of detainees at the KP Dom. Fifth ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error of fact by concluding that the cruel treatment which represented inhumane treatment and cruel treatment was not inflicted for discriminatory reasons and that therefore Krnojelac could not be held responsible for persecutions as a superior. I think I'm speaking too fast. I apologise. Sixth ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly erred in acquitting Krnojelac of persecution under forced labour. Seventh ground of appeal: The Trial Chamber allegedly committed an error by acquitting Krnojelac of the charge of persecution under deportation. For that seventh ground, the Prosecutor put forward several arguments. First, was that there was an error of law by stating that the movement over national borders was an element which is constituent -- a constituent element of expulsion. Second, the Trial Chamber which will be an error of fact because it judged that 35 Muslim detainees transferred toward Montenegro left of their own will. Third, an error of fact. The Trial Chamber found that the transfer of the 35 Muslim detainees toward Montenegro was not inspired by discriminatory reasons. Fourth, an error was made by -- an error was made by stating that Krnojelac was not guilty of persecution, deportation for the transfer of some of the detainees towards other places in Bosnia. Fifth, the Trial Chamber committed an error by judging that Krnojelac was not responsible under Article 7(1) of the Statute for expulsion and expulsions which are constituent of persecution. These are the grounds as we put -- the Appeals Chamber has put them together. The Chamber also recalls that the two appellants have appealed against the sentence. I would now ask the parties to pay attention, because before we hear your arguments about the alleged errors, the Appeals Chamber considers that some precision should be made about the criterion applicable to the review of the observations of the Trial Chamber. As the Appeals Chamber has pointed out on many occasions, the appeal is not the occasion for the parties to replead their case. This is not a de novo trial. On appeal the parties must limit their arguments to the questions which fall within the framework of Article 25 of our Statute. In general, the Appeals Chamber does not hear any arguments but those founded on errors of law which have been claimed which would invalidate the judgement. As regards -- or on errors of fact which would have caused a miscarriage of justice. Only exceptionally, when a party might raise a question of general interest for the case law of the Tribunal. That would be the only case. Only in that case does the Trial Chamber considered that it would be proper to make an exception to the rule. In this case, the very great majority of the grounds raised by the appellants deal with alleged errors of fact. I would ask you to pay attention to this now, because this is going to -- this is going to form the basis and the ground -- limits of our discussions. The Appeals Chamber recalls that in this -- that in this case we recall the appellant, according to well-established -- I apologise to the interpreters for going very fast. I always look at the watch and we have two days, so I tend to speak fast. Let me speak more slowly. In this case, the great majority of the grounds raised by the appellants have to do with errors of fact that have been claimed. The Appeals Chamber recalls that in this case the charge -- the responsibility of the -- for the appellant is, according to well-established case law the following: For the Appeals Chamber to invalidate an observation of the Trial Chamber, an applicant must demonstrate that it had committed an error of fact and that there was a failure in justice as result. Consequently, the applicant must give double proof that there was an error of fact and there was a miscarriage of justice that resulted from that. The error is demonstrated when the appellant shows that no Judge or court of reasonable fact could have reached the decision which is being challenged. The appellant must also prove that the error of fact weighed heavily on the decision of the Trial Chamber and that there -- was therefore a miscarriage of justice. The proof that was -- must be brought by the applicant also involves precision in respect of the Trial Chamber's conclusions which are being contested. For this hearing, I will ask the parties to be very precise and to be rigorous in their development relating to the grounds of appeal and to make an effective use of the book of authorities. These positions now should give you the framework for our discussions. If necessary, we will recall this to you. Let me give you -- explain the organisation of our work as follows from a Scheduling Order for this hearing. We agree that the Prosecutor will begin with the presentation of its arguments and will have one hour and 30 minutes. We were to start at 9.00, so we will start at 9.15 and we will deduct the missing time and take a break then. And then the Prosecutor will continue for another hour. So that means the Prosecutor will have two and a half hours. And we will adjust the schedule to the little delay that we have right now. We will take a break of -- two-hour break around lunch-time and then we will give the floor to the Defence. The Defence will have two hours as well, which will be broken by a 30-minute pause. And finally, the Prosecutor will finish the work by giving her reply for 30 minutes. Tomorrow, that is the 15th of May, we will also begin at 9.00, and the Defence will present its arguments for two hours with a 30-minute break. We will also have a two-hour break for lunch and then the Prosecutor will have two hours also with a break of 30 minutes, but I will explain this again as the time moves along, and finally, we'll have the Defence reply. And we will complete our work. Without anything further ado, if there are no particular comments to be made, I give the floor to the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has provided to the Chamber an order of appearance. I believe the members of the Bench would have it. As it indicates, I propose now to deal with the first and second of the Prosecution's grounds of appeal to which Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, has referred. Following that, my colleague Ms. Brady will deal with grounds 3 and 5. Ms. Norul Rashid will then present the submissions on grounds 7 and 6, and finally Mr. Carmona will present the Prosecution's arguments on grounds 4 and 8, ground 8 being the appeal against sentence. With the Chamber's permission then, without more ado, I will proceed to the Prosecution's first ground of appeal which is that the Trial Chamber erred in law in its determination of the elements of common purpose or joint criminal enterprise. This ground of appeal relates specifically to two of the respondent's convictions in which he was found to be individually criminally liable under Article 7(1) of the Statute, in respect of imprisonment and in respect of living conditions in the camp. However, he was convicted as an aider and abettor only. The Prosecution submission is that he was liable for committing these crimes as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, and the Prosecution seeks to have the verdict amended accordingly. It also seeks an increase in sentence to reflect the increased responsibility of the respondent in that respect. To summarise very briefly, there are two principal errors which the Prosecution contends were made in the Trial Chamber's judgement in this respect. In the Tadic appeal judgement, the Appeals Chamber said that there were three elements of the actus reus for liability under joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution's submission is that on the findings of the Trial Chamber, the first and third of these elements were satisfied. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber fell into error in its definition and application of the second of those elements. Secondly, the Tadic appeals judgement, at paragraph 228, set out the mens rea for liability as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise and the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in defining and applying the mens rea. For convenience, I propose to deal first with the conviction in respect of imprisonment. I will revert subsequently in respect to the living conditions in the camp. In respect of the unlawful imprisonment, the respondent was convicted as an aider and abettor on count 1 for persecution as a crime against humanity under Article 5(H) of the Statute. He was also found liable as an aider and abettor under count 11, which was imprisonment as a crime against humanity under Article 5(E). He was not convicted on count 11 because it was held that that would have been impermissibly cumulative, but nonetheless, the Trial Chamber's findings on count 11 are important as they form the basis of the findings in respect of count 1. The Trial Chamber's factual findings are set out in paragraphs 116 to 124 of the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 124 that non-Serb civilian men were detained at the KP Dom because they were Muslim. At paragraph 118, it was held that they were imprisoned indiscriminately. At paragraphs 122, it was said that they were detained arbitrarily and with no legal basis under national or international law. The Trial Chamber's findings in these paragraphs are summarised in paragraph 438 of the trial judgement in which it said that during the period relevant to this indictment, non-Serbs were illegally imprisoned at the KP Dom, and this imprisonment was effected primarily or solely with the intent to discriminate against them because of their religious affiliations. The Trial Chamber further found at paragraph 50 that the detention of non-Serbs in the KP Dom and the acts or omissions which took place therein were clearly related to the widespread and systematic attack against the non-Serb civilian population in the Foca municipality. It's submitted that it's clear from these findings that the Trial Chamber accepted the Prosecution's contention that the imprisonment of non-Serb civilian men resulted from a joint criminal enterprise. This is clear from paragraph 127 of the Trial Chamber where the Trial Chamber refers to "the joint criminal enterprise to illegally imprison the non-Serb detainees." Subsequently in the same paragraph, there's a reference to "that joint criminal enterprise." There is a subsequent additional reference to "the joint criminal enterprise," and the Trial Chamber also refers in that paragraph to the respondent being aware of his contribution to the maintenance of "that unlawful system" by the principal offenders. It's submitted that there is no doubt that the Trial Chamber was satisfied of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. And although the Trial Chamber doesn't expressly spell out how it concluded that there was such a joint criminal enterprise, it's clear that this stemmed in part from the widespread and systematic nature of the detentions. In footnote 353, the Trial Chamber refers to the "systematic and collective nature" of the detention of the Muslim male population. And in paragraph 41, it says that the "illegal arrest and imprisonment of non-Serb males was carried out on a massive scale and in a systematic way." It's evident that such a systematic campaign of detention could not be the result of the actions of a single person or of the actions of various individuals acting independently; it could only be the result of organised conduct, in other words, of a joint enterprise. Now, not only did the Trial Chamber find that there was a joint criminal enterprise, but it found that the respondent knew of it. At paragraph 62, it made the finding that the accused did in fact know that the Muslim civilian population were systematically targeted and abused in many ways, that he knew that prison camps for the detention of Muslims were set up in other municipalities of the area, and that he knew that the mistreatment which occurred at the KP Dom was part of the attack upon the non-Serb population of Foca town and municipality. At paragraph 127, it also found that the respondent knew that his acts and omissions were contributing to the maintenance of that unlawful system by the principal offenders. Now, before addressing his liability under the law of joint criminal enterprise, it's necessary to recall that in the Tadic appeal judgement, the Appeals Chamber found that there are three categories of joint criminal enterprise liability, and it's submitted that this threefold categorisation is now a part of the Trial Chamber's jurisprudence. I'd refer additionally to the Kayishema and Ruzindana appeal judgement at paragraph 193, and the Kordic and Cerkez judgement at paragraphs 397 and 398. Now, the third of these categories can be left aside for the purposes of this ground of appeal, although it does arise again in the Prosecution's second ground of appeal. In relation to the first two categories of joint criminal enterprise liability, there appears to be some suggestion in paragraph 78 of the trial judgement that there may in fact be no real difference between those categories, and this conflation of the first two categories into a single category is dealt with in paragraphs 215 to 221 of the Prosecution appeal brief. But it's submitted that the distinction between the two categories is this: The first category of joint criminal enterprise cases is where the joint criminal enterprise exists to commit a specific criminal act. And to give a hypothetical example, if one supposes that four accused set out with the purpose of killing a specific individual and each of them has the intent that the victim be killed and each plays a role in that killing, then each will be equally liable for having committed that murder within the meaning of Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute, even though the mens rea -- even though the actus reus of that killing may have been performed by only one of the four. The second category of joint criminal enterprise cases, in our submission, was described -- although described by the Appeals Chamber as the concentration camp cases, is not confined necessarily to concentration camps. The concentration camp cases may have been a reference to the kind of post-World War II cases that were identified as falling within that category, but the Prosecution submits that the real essence of this category is that, unlike the first which contemplates the commission of a specific crime, in this second category the joint criminal enterprise is an ongoing system over a period of time which continues and which contemplates the commission of various undefined crimes in the course of that system. A concentration camp may be an example of such a system but not necessarily the only one. As I said, the legal elements for this form of liability are set out in paragraph 227 of the Tadic appeal judgement and paragraph 2.3 of the Prosecution appeal brief. The first requirement is a plurality of persons who need not be organised in a military, political, or administrative structure, and that requirement is clearly satisfied in the circumstances of this case. Now, the second requirement -- and here, as I say, is the first error, we submit, in the Trial judgement. The second requirement, as articulated in the Tadic appeal judgement is the existence of a common plan, design, or purpose which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute. And the Appeals Chamber goes on to say there is no necessity for this plan, design, or purpose to have been previously arranged or formulated, and proceeds to give some further explanation. Now, in relation to this requirement, the Trial Chamber said at paragraph 80 that a joint criminal enterprise exists where there is an understanding or arrangement amounting to an agreement between two or more persons that they will commit a crime. And then in paragraphs 170, 315, 346, and 487, the Trial Chamber looks to whether there was evidence of an agreement between the respondent and other guards and military authorities for the commission of certain crimes in the KP Dom. Paragraph 487 is particularly significant because it looks for an agreement to commit persecution and the conviction in respect of unlawful detention was a conviction for persecution. In our submission, this requirement of an agreement is not part of this element of joint criminal enterprise liability. It will be seen that in the wording from the Tadic appeal judgement, the word "agreement" is not used. The Trial Chamber, in footnote 235 of the trial judgement, refers to two decisions in support of this requirement of an agreement, but it's noteworthy that none of the passages there cited in fact use the word "agreement" either. In the Prosecution's submission, in cases of systemic joint criminal enterprises, it's quite likely that many of the participants in the enterprise will not know of the identities of other participants. Indeed, they may not even be aware as new people come on board and join the criminal enterprise; they may not be aware as people leave. What in our submission is the crucial requirement is the existence of a common plan, design, or purpose which may be a system. If an accused knows of the existence of a system and knows that the system involves the commission of crimes, the accused by knowingly becoming a part of that system and contributing significantly to it, with the purpose or intent of furthering that system, in our submission this second requirement of joint criminal enterprise liability is satisfied. And in our submission, the rationale for that might be explained by analogy with the mob violence cases. In cases of mob violence, it may be a group of people set out and, for instance, beat a victim to death but it may not be known exactly who struck blows in the course of that incident or indeed who struck the fatal blow, and yet if each had the common intent of beating the victim to death, each will be equally liable for having committed the murder. In the case of a system, a systemic joint criminal enterprise, in our submission it's not necessary to identify who the planner or who the instigator of this plan was. If it was possible to identify that, that person might be charged for planning or inciting, but if it's clear that a system exists, and if it is clear that a person is part of that system contributing significantly to it with the intent of furthering that system, in our submission there is a common purpose and that the accused in that case has the intent of furthering that purpose. And the second requirement of joint criminal enterprise liability will be met. To move then to the third requirement of the actus reus of joint criminal enterprise liability, this was defined by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic appeal judgement of participation of the accused in common design involving the perpetration of one of the crimes provided for in the Statute. And it goes on to note that "the accused's participation need not itself require the commission of any specific crime but may take the form of assistance in or contribution to the execution of the common plan or purpose." And in our submission, there is a clear finding by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 127 that the respondent knew that his acts and omissions were contributing to that unlawful purpose by the principal offenders. The other requirement then is the mens rea requirement for this form of liability. And at paragraph 228 of the Tadic appeal judgement, the Appeals Chamber said that the mens rea in the second category of joint criminal enterprise liability is personal knowledge of the system of ill treatment whether by express testimony or as a matter of reasonable inference from the accused's position of authority as well as intent to further this common concerted system of ill treatment. The Prosecution accepts that the distinction between an aider and abettor and a participant in a joint criminal enterprise is that an aider and abettor need not share the intent of the criminal enterprise. And the question then in this case is: Did the respondent share the intent of the joint criminal enterprise? Now, I refer again to the express findings of the Trial Chamber. In particular, paragraph 62, that the accused knew of the attack upon the non-Serb civilian population of Foca and surrounding areas. Paragraph 124, that he knew that they were imprisoned because they were Muslim. And at paragraph 127, that the accused knew that the imprisonment of the non-Serb detainees was unlawful and that he knew that his acts and omission were contributing to the maintenance of that unlawful system by the principal offenders. Now, why did the Trial Chamber find that the mens rea requirement had not been satisfied? It addresses this also in paragraph 127 of the trial judgement. It says: "The Trial Chamber is not satisfied that the only reasonable inference which can be drawn from these facts is that the accused shared the intent of that joint criminal enterprise. In particular, the Trial Chamber does not consider that the Prosecution has excluded the reasonable possibility that the accused was merely carrying out the orders given to him by those who appointed him to the position of warden at the KP Dom without sharing their criminal intent." Now, the possibility that the respondent may have merely been carrying out orders, in our submission, must be entirely irrelevant given that Article 7(4) of the Tribunal's Statute expressly provides that superior orders is no defence, even if it may be relevant for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: So the question comes down to simply whether the respondent shared the intent. And the Prosecution submits that there is a well-established distinction in criminal law between intent and motive. One imagines, for instance, an accused who participates on several occasions in the commission of armed bank robberies together with other perpetrators and whose role is to stand there silently holding a gun at the bank staff while others demand money and collect it. If he were to say that he did not share the intent of the bank robbery merely because his reason for participating was he wanted his friends not to ostracise him from their group or that he was concerned that he would be unemployed if he didn't become a member of this group, clearly his motive for doing this is irrelevant. In circumstances like that, it is clear that he shares the intent of the criminal enterprise to commit armed bank robbery. Support for this proposition might be found, for instance, by reference to Article 30 of the Statute of the International Criminal Court. Article 30, paragraph 2 says that "for the purposes of this Article, a person has intent where in relation to conduct, the person means to engage in that conduct." Clearly the case here. In relation to a consequence, that the person means to cause that consequence or is aware that it will occur in the ordinary course of events. In this respect, we submit that it's important to underscore that direct evidence of a state of mind is usually difficult to obtain, and the mens rea in any circumstances is normally inferred from surrounding circumstances. And authorities for that proposition would be the Celebici Trial Chamber judgement at paragraphs 437 and 439. An example where this occurred in a joint criminal enterprise case of the first category would be the Furundzija appeal judgement at paragraph 120 where it was said that, "where the act of one accused contributes to the purpose of the other and both acted simultaneously in the same place and within full view of the other over a prolonged period of time, the argument that there was no common purpose is plainly unsustainable." In the case of a joint criminal enterprise of the second category, an example that can be cited is the Kvocka Trial Chamber where at paragraph 271 it is said that, "the shared intent may and often will be inferred knowledge of the plan and participation in its advancement." At paragraph 278, it's said that, "an intent so as to rise to the level of co-perpetration may also be inferred from knowledge of the crimes being perpetrated and continued participation which enables the camp's functioning." At paragraph 249, it's said that, "an aider or abettor of a joint criminal enterprise whose acts originally assist, or otherwise facilitate the criminal endeavour, may become so involved in its operations that he may graduate to the status of a co-perpetrator." At paragraph 284, it's said that, "this may occur if the participation lasts for an extensive period or if the accused becomes more directly involved in the functioning of the enterprise." At paragraphs 290 to 292, the Kvocka Trial Chamber suggested that the level of superiority in the hierarchy may be relevant to determining whether the accused was a principal or an aider and abettor. And other pertinent observations on the significance of a contribution can be found in that Trial Chamber at paragraphs 306, 311, and 312. In other words, we submit that where a person over a protracted period of time intentionally performs acts which contribute substantially to the joint criminal enterprise and knows of the joint criminal enterprise and knows that the acts are contributing substantially to it, then regardless of motive, in our submission, that would constitute intent for the purposes of the criminal law. Now, what were the facts of this case? The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 96 that the respondent was the warden of the KP Dom from 18th of April, 1992, until at least the end of July, 1993. That's 15 months. It found, at paragraph 107, that the accused exercised supervisory responsibility over all subordinate personnel and detainees at the prison. It found, most pertinently we submit, at paragraph 100 that he voluntarily accepted this position. It found at paragraph 102 that he had the power to instigate and take disciplinary measures. At paragraph 103, that he had responsibility for ensuring that detainees did not escape. Again at paragraph 103, that the respondent exercised final control over the work of the detainees. At paragraph 126, that he held the most senior position within the KP Dom and that he did allow civilians to be detained there knowing that their detention was unlawful. And at paragraph 171, that he contributed in a substantial way to the continued maintenance of the conditions in the camp by giving encouragement to the principal offenders. In our submission on those findings of fact, the only reasonable conclusion is that the accused, in accordance with the definition of intent under international criminal law, shared the intent of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution submits that if the reasoning of the Trial Chamber in this case were correct, it would mean that every official in a persecutory regime, one could cite, for instance, Nazi Germany, who contributed significantly to the atrocities committed by that regime but did not directly commit any crime could under contemporary international law escape liability as a principal and be only an aider and abettor by saying, "I was simply doing my job." The result would be that the low-level perpetrators who physically commit the crimes would be found liable as perpetrators and the senior, more superior people would be mere aiders and abettors, and we submit that cannot be the case. With the Chamber's permission, I turn then to the second aspect of this ground of appeal which relates to the conviction in respect of the living conditions in the camp. The accused was convicted in respect of the living conditions again on count 1, persecution as a crime against humanity, also count 15, for cruel treatment in respect of the living conditions. In relation to these counts, the Trial Chamber expressly rejected, at paragraphs 170 and also paragraph 490, the Prosecution's case that the respondent was responsible for these crimes as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise. As I have mentioned, at paragraph 170 it's said that there would have to be an agreement between the respondent and guards in the camp and military authorities to commit these inhumane conditions. For the reasons I've already submitted, an agreement is not necessary. The question is: Was the -- The question is: Did the joint criminal enterprise, which I've already said the Trial Chamber found did exist in relation to the unlawful imprisonment, did that joint criminal enterprise extend also to the imposition of inhumane living conditions on detainees in the camp? Now, I put the question in this way for a reason. It's because the Trial Chamber took the approach of looking for a separate joint criminal enterprise in relation to each of the different kinds of crimes committed. At paragraph 315, the Trial Chamber looked for an agreement for a joint criminal enterprise to commit beatings. At paragraph 346, the Trial Chamber looked for an agreement for a joint criminal enterprise to commit murder. At paragraph 427, it looked at whether there was any joint criminal enterprise that may have existed to enslave the non-Serb detainees. Now, this approach of the Trial Chamber of slicing a joint criminal enterprise into a number of separate joint criminal enterprises is dealt with in paragraphs 222 to 230 of the Prosecution appeal brief. But Prosecution submits that this is a wholly artificial and unrealistic analysis. All of the crimes occurred in the same place, at the same time, against the same victim group in the same detention facility of which the respondent was the warden. The Trial Chamber found that the unlawful imprisonment was effected by a joint criminal enterprise. From there, the question is whether the enterprise extended to inhumane living conditions; and in the Prosecution's submission, that is the only reasonable conclusion. At paragraph 134, the Trial Chamber found that there was a deliberate policy of isolating detainees in the KP Dom. At paragraph 135, it found that non-Serb detainees were deliberately housed in cramped conditions. At paragraph 138, it said that it was satisfied that the suffering of the non-Serb detainees during 1992 was the result of a deliberate policy on the part of those in charge of the KP Dom. At paragraph 139, it said that there was a deliberate policy to feed the non-Serb detainees barely enough for their survival. At paragraph 140, it said that there was a deliberate policy of withholding available medical supplies for non-Serb detainees. In our submission, such deliberate policies again cannot be the result of acts of individuals acting alone or of numbers of different individuals each acting individually. They can only be the result of a joint enterprise; and given the unity of time, place, victim group, the only reasonable conclusion was that it was part of the same joint criminal enterprise as the unlawful imprisonment. Now, that deals with the two counts to which this ground of appeal relates, and although unnecessary to decide for the purposes of this ground of appeal, on the facts as found, in our submission, other crimes committed in the camp were clearly also part of the same joint criminal enterprise. In relation to the beatings, at paragraph 248 the Trial Chamber found that they took place on a frequent and systematic basis. At paragraph 311 it referred to the widespread nature of the beatings. At paragraph 273 it described a consistent pattern of conduct in relation to the beatings in the camp, and this pattern is referred to again at paragraphs 264 and 275. The same reasoning, we submit, would apply to the killings. The Trial Chamber found that the killings followed a pattern, which is described in paragraphs 333 to paragraphs 335. Again, such a systemic pattern cannot be the result of acts of individuals; it can only be the result of a joint criminal enterprise. Similarly, the forced labour. There is no dispute in this case that there was an organised labour programme at the KP Dom, and for the reasons that will be given by my colleague Ms. Rashid, we submit that in the circumstances of the KP Dom, no valid consent could be given by the detainees to undertake the labour, therefore there was a systematic campaign of forced labour. In relation to the deportations, we refer to paragraph 49 of the trial judgement where the Trial Chamber found that the expulsion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: My apologies to the translators. Paragraph 49 of the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber found that the expulsion, exchange, or deportation of non-Serbs, including detainees at the KP Dom, was the final stage of the Serb attack upon the non-Serb civilian population in Foca municipality. And towards the end of the paragraph it said: "In late 1994, the last remaining Muslim detainees at the KP Dom were exchanged, marking the end of the attack upon those civilians and the achievement of a Serbian region ethnically cleansed of Muslims. By the end of the war in 1995, Foca had become an almost purely Serb town." The deportations, in our submission, can only be regarded as the result of a joint criminal enterprise, and again, given the unity in time, place, and victim group, the only reasonable inference is that it was part of the same joint criminal enterprise as the unlawful detention, living conditions, and other crimes that were committed. Unless I can assist the Chamber further, those are the Prosecution's submissions in relation to the first ground of appeal. With the Chamber's permission, I would then move to the second ground of appeal. The Prosecution's second ground of appeal relates to the finding in paragraphs 84 to 86 of the trial judgement that the accused could not be held liable for the extended form of joint criminal enterprise liability unless the extended form of this liability was pleaded in the indictment. The background to this ground of appeal is that at trial, the Prosecution submitted a second amended indictment pleading a common purpose case, following which the respondent filed a preliminary motion under Rule 72, complaining that the indictment was insufficiently precise in relation to certain details. In a decision on this Defence preliminary motion dated 11th of May, 2000, the Trial Chamber denied this preliminary motion, but in its decision, it referred in paragraph 11 to the three categories of joint criminal enterprise cases identified in the Tadic appeal judgement, following which it added, and I quote: "As the indictment is silent on the subject, it is unnecessary for present purposes to consider the last of those categories." Now, the Prosecution trial team didn't understand this to mean that it was required to amend the indictment if it intended to rely on that third category. And in fact in its pre-trial brief, dated the 16th of October 2000, the Prosecution referred in footnote 23 to that interlocutory decision and said that the Trial Chamber had recognised the relevance of at least the first two categories of joint criminal enterprise liability and stated that the Prosecution asserted that all three categories applied. And then paragraphs 57 to 63 of that pre-trial brief dealt with the third category. The Prosecution's argument, just to explain, was that the accused had allowed outsiders to enter into the KP Dom and that it was a natural and foreseeable consequence of allowing them in that beatings and other acts of mistreatment would be the consequence. The same contention was raised again in the Prosecutor's final trial brief, dated 13th of July, 2001, in which it also relied on this third category. Nevertheless, in the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber held, at paragraph 86, that in the exercise of its discretion in light of its own express interpretation that only a basic form of joint criminal enterprise had been pleaded, the Prosecution would not be allowed to rely upon the extended form. The Prosecution submits that there was an error in so holding. I point out that as the Prosecution does not rely on this third category in this appeal, it is not necessary to decide strictly, but the Prosecution raises it as a ground of general importance to the case law of the Tribunal. The reasons are set out in the appeal brief of the Prosecution, and I have very little to add. Our basic proposition is that the right of an accused under Article 18(4) of the Statute -- sorry, under Article 21(4)(a) is "to be informed promptly and in detail in a language he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him," and this right is given effect by Article 18(4) of the Statute and Rule 47(c) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which require the indictment to contain a precise statement of facts and the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged. And the crimes, in our submission, mean the substantive crimes under Article 2 to 5 of the Statute, not modes of liability under Article 7(1). For that proposition, we rely on the Celebici appeal judgement at paragraph 351. In that case, the indictment had charged the accused with participating in certain crimes. The accused argued that as he had not been expressly charged with aiding and abetting, he could not be convicted of aiding and abetting. And the Appeals Chamber said, at paragraph 351, that the word "participation" here is broad enough to encompass all forms of responsibility which are included within Article 7(1) and that although greater specificity in drafting indictments is desirable, failing to identify expressly the exact mode of participation is not necessarily fatal. And it also pointed out that no complaint had been made prior to trial about this, that the accused -- no complaint that did he not know the case that he had to meet and that it was too late to raise the complaint at that point. I would make three points arising out of this decision. First, it's clear that an indictment is not necessarily defective merely because it pleads Article 7(1) in general terms without specifying any mode of liability. And joint criminal enterprise, in our submission, is clearly a mode of liability under Article 7(1) and would be included in any such formulation. And for the same reason, if an indictment expressly alleges joint criminal enterprise liability, in the absence of some indication to the contrary, it must be taken to include all three categories. Secondly, the question is not whether the mode of liability is pleaded but whether the accused is given sufficient notice of the case he has to meet. And thirdly, this decision of the Appeals Chamber, in our submission, stands for the proposition that any objections have to be raised at the appropriate time. The Appeals Chamber in the Celebici appeals judgement applied the waiver rule that an objection could cannot be raised for the first time on an appeal, but in our submission, that is an application of the broader principle that any objection has to be raised at the appropriate time. Objections to defects in the form of the indictment are to be raised at the pre-trial stage. In our submission, if an indictment clearly includes in a general formulation a particular mode of liability, the accused knows what's included. It would be too late to raise an objection, for instance, in the final trial brief. Just to conclude with a practical example, the example of a case where the third category of joint criminal enterprise liability has been applied was in the Tadic case. If one looks at the way the indictment in the Tadic case was pleaded, paragraph 12 of that indictment said that on about the 14th of June, 1992, armed Serbs including Dusko Tadic entered the area of Jaskici, that armed Serbs killed a certain number of victims as a result of which Dusko Tadic committed murder. It's submitted that on that wording, it's perfectly clear that the Prosecution case must either be that the accused personally committed the killings or that the armed group referred to had the joint common purpose of committing the killings or that the armed group referred to had a joint other criminal purpose but that the killings were the natural and foreseeable consequence of that. In our submission, it may not be known until all the evidence is in precisely what the position was and that the Defence would not be materially assisted simply by mechanically pleading all forms of liability under Article 7(1). An indictment is not required to plead evidence. It's not required to plead the law. It's required to plead the facts, and the facts put the Defence on sufficient notice of what the case is that needs to be met. In our submission, the indictment is valid and all charges within it must be considered by the Trial Chamber. In this case, in our submission, there was no complaint made by the Defence at the appropriate time despite the fact that this form of liability was relied on expressly in the Prosecution pre-trial brief. There has been no showing that the Defence was prejudiced by this. And in our submission, as a matter of law, the Trial Chamber was in error in refusing to consider this form of liability. And unless I can be of further assistance, they are the submissions on the Prosecution's second ground of appeal. With the Appeals Chamber's leave, I would invite you to call upon my colleague Ms. Brady to continue the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, and Your Honours. This morning, I'll be addressing two grounds of the Prosecution appeal, the third ground of appeal on torture and the fifth ground of appeal which is persecution based on beatings. Your Honours, both grounds of appeal relate to the beatings that happened in KP Dom, and more specifically to Krnojelac's criminal liability under Article 7(3) for 50 or so beatings which were established by the Trial Chamber as occurring in the KP Dom at the relevant time during his term, Krnojelac's term as warden and which reached a level of seriousness or gravity so as to amount to cruel treatment and inhumane acts. Before I turn to each ground separately, I would like to point out that there is a significant difference in the two areas, in the timing of when these errors occurred. The error on torture occurred at the 7(3) stage of the court's analysis. Even though 14 of the beatings which were established met all the legal requirements, all the legal elements for the crime of torture, the Trial Chamber limited Krnojelac's superior responsibility for these beatings to cruel treatment and inhumane acts only. And as I'll show you, as we've already set out our submissions in the brief and as I plan to take you through some of the salient points in our brief, this was through a fundamentally flawed application of the Celebici had-reason-to-know test for mens rea for 7(3) liability. On the other hand, the error regarding persecution based on beatings was at an earlier stage of analysis and one could call it at the stage of crime base analysis. Though more than 50 -- 50 to 60 beatings were established on the evidence, the Trial Chamber found only two, only two of these beatings were persecution, and these on political grounds. For all of the other beatings which were established and there is a sizable number of beatings that that relates to, the Trial Chamber, and this is -- was wrongly, in our view, was not satisfied that they were persecutory and we say -- our submission is that this was due to a wholly erroneous evaluation of the evidence, and in particular, its complete failure to consider and make proper inferences from the systematically discriminatory environment of the KP Dom in which all the beatings occurred. Turning first to the third ground of appeal on torture. In our submission, the proper adjudication of Krnojelac's liability under 7(3) for these 14 -- I'll call them torture beatings, should be just as that, as torture. He should be convicted under counts 2 and 4 for torture and not under counts 5 and 7 for cruel treatment and inhumane acts. And we also submit that this increase in the gravity -- in the crime base -- in the crimes for which he should bear responsibility should be reflected accordingly in his sentence. How exactly did the Trial Chamber err? It was by finding that even though Krnojelac knew - and let's remember we're talking about actually knew - that widespread beatings were going on in KP Dom. This did not give him reason to know that some beatings may have been conducted for a prohibited purpose of torture. And, Your Honours, I take you to the findings of the Trial Chamber in its judgement relating to how he had actual knowledge of the beatings, and there in paragraphs 309 to 311 and, as well, paragraph 316. In the circumstances of this detention centre, how could a Trial Chamber conclude that he was not placed on notice of the risk of torture? And we must remember that we're not speaking about -- we're not -- the torture we speak of is not some wholly different form of conduct. In reality, what we're talking about is a deliberate and aggravated form of the beatings. Some of those beatings met that criteria of being deliberate and aggravated and, hence, torture. Our proposition is a very simple one. Applying Celebici to the facts of this case can lead to only one reasonable conclusion, and that is that by actually knowing of the beatings going on within KP Dom, he was on notice of the risk that at least some of them may have resulted in torture. His knowledge of the beatings in this KP Dom environment was enough to alert him to the need for additional information or to conduct an investigation to ascertain whether torture by beatings was being committed by his subordinates. This fits squarely within the Celebici test, and we know from that case which has been endorsed by -- the test has been endorsed by this Chamber in the Celebici Appeals Chamber judgement as well as more recently in the case of Bagilishema. We know that the information which puts a superior on notice doesn't need to point conclusively to the existence of crimes, only to the need for some further action. And it doesn't -- nor does it need to point to specific crimes. And we know this. This is best summarised by the Appeals Chamber itself in Celebici at paragraph 238 when it said: "A showing that a superior had some general information in his possession which would put him on notice of possible unlawful acts by his subordinates would be sufficient to prove that he had reason to know. This information does not need to provide specific information about unlawful acts committed or about to be committed." And this is what leads the Appeals Chamber to give the example in Celebici of the commander who knows his soldiers are of a violent disposition or have been drinking before a mission, he can be said to have reason to know that his subordinates may commit crimes and will be responsible for those crimes on that basis. Nor does the superior need to be in actual possession of the information about the crimes committed by the subordinates. It's sufficient if he was provided with the relevant information. Even if the information was made available to him. If the information is objectively alarming, his duty to inquire or to investigate, thereby, is triggered. And as I said before, this has been endorsed by the Appeals Chamber in Celebici and in Bagilishema, and in particular in Bagilishema, it was -- the Chamber there has held that this test applies equally to military and civilian superiors. Our submission is that when a person is the warden of such a prison as this for 15 months, who has an office right in the centre of the complex, who is told by at least one detainee, the witness RJ, that the detainees could hear the sounds of beatings, who personally saw one detainee, the detainee Ekrem Zekovic, being beaten as punishment for an attempted escape, and who had every opportunity to observe the physical manifestations of the widespread and brutal beatings which the Trial Chamber itself said must have been obvious to everyone, and when all of this -- when all of this is considered against the fact that he knew the discriminatory nature of the imprisonment and of the discriminatory nature of the inhumane living conditions for the detainees, and indeed he knew that the interrogations in the camp were pervasive, that interrogators were coming in and out, interrogations could be said to have been a daily feature or at least a very frequent feature of life in the KP Dom, with all these facts, the only reasonable conclusion must be that he was placed on notice of the risk of torture. I don't need to remind Your Honours that the cornerstone of superior responsibility is in failing to do anything in the face of adequate information. And again, to quote from the Celebici Appeals Chamber: "The point is not that knowledge may be presumed if a person fails in his duty to obtain the relevant information of a crime but that it may be presumed if he had the means to obtain the knowledge but deliberately refrained from doing so." And that's the exact situation that we have here. This is -- the analysis that we say should be applied -- should have been applied by the Trial Chamber is the very one which was used to find Mucic himself liable under Article 7(3) for six tortures -- for many crimes in Celebici, but including six tortures in the Celebici camp. The Trial Chamber found that since Mucic knew or had reason to know of -- that violations of international humanitarian law were going on, this was sufficient inquiry notice making him liable for all the crimes in the camp, including torture. And this was upheld in the Appeals Chamber. I also would invite Your Honours to look at the application of 7(3), the test on reason to know under 7(3). When the Trial Chamber, the Krnojelac Trial Chamber applies this test in relation to persecutory beatings -- you will recall the two persecutory beatings were actually established as happening in the camp, and when they came to apply the reason-to-know test to find him responsible for these persecutory beatings in relation to two detainees, it correctly applied the test in the way we say they should have for the torture beatings. And I would invite Your Honours to look in particular at paragraphs 493 and 497 to 498 of the judgement. In particular, the Trial Chamber held in 493 that the Prosecution must prove that the accused had information in his possession sufficient to put him on notice as to the commission of the underlying offence and its commission on discriminatory grounds. But see how they apply the test, and that's in 497 to 498. Had the accused, they say - the Trial Chamber says - had the accused acted upon information within his possession with respect to beatings, any investigation would have made clear to him the discriminatory nature -- the discriminatory intent of the principal offender. Your Honours, I would also invite you to look at the treatment of two detainees in particular. We've fully set out our arguments on this in our appeal brief at paragraphs 436 to 438 in relation to the detainee Dzemo Balic in paragraph 5.15 of the indictment and then what happened to him in the isolation cell immediately following, which was the incident before. Just to very briefly summarise to show you this inconsistent and wrong application of 7(3), Dzemo Balic was taken out of the canteen line and then severely beaten by two KP Dom guards in the administration building. At the time that the beating occurred, one of the guards made a comment to the effect of, "Oh, you're the one who promised Alija eight kilogrammes of Serbian eyes." And he was severely beaten at this time, and then later he was put into the isolation cell for about 20 days and further questioned, and the questions were basically concerning his SDA -- his activities as a member or alleged member of the SDA and where weapons were and drawing up lists and the like. Well, in relation to the first part of what happened, the initial beating, there the Trial Chamber found, well, yes, it is persecution and made him responsible under 7(3). But what happened to him later, which was literally just a continuum really of his first beating, what happened to him later was classified as torture. And for this particular aspect of his beating, he did not bear 7(3) responsibility for that. So I think that one example does draw out an inconsistent approach by the Trial Chamber and also a wrong application of 7(3) when it comes to torture. And I won't go into it now, but there's another very compelling example in relation to the witness FWS-03 and his two other co-victims, Dedovic and Sabanovic, in paragraph 5.23. In sum, Your Honours, our submission is that Krnojelac should not be entitled to evade the full scope of liability by doing nothing in the face of information which was clearly sufficient to place him on notice of the risk of torture. And indeed, to make such a finding runs completely counter to the very heart, indeed the very raison d'etre of superior responsibility. Those, Your Honours, are my submissions on torture. If I can be of assistance on that ground. Otherwise, I can turn immediately to the fifth ground, which is persecution based on beatings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, should I understand your presentation this way: That you're saying the accused knew of the beatings and he knew that interrogations were going on and, therefore, these things were sufficient to put him on notice of a risk that the beatings were for the purpose of eliciting the information required by the interrogations? Is that the way you state your case?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I, in addition, ask why in this case do you refer to 7(3) responsibility only in line with that what we heard beforehand by your colleague? Couldn't it be also the case, based on the case law, that there would be a 7(1) responsibility as co-perpetrator, knowing about that what was going on, but participating but not intervening. So committing in the sense of omitting because allegedly, I take it that it would be your case, that he had the duty to intervene and, therefore, the question once again, why not 7(1) responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Indeed we would say that he could equally have been responsible on a 7(1) theory for these crimes, and we would use the same analysis as used by the Trial Chamber seen most clearly in paragraph 316 of the judgement where they actually made the finding in relation to just beatings per se, beatings as cruel treatment or inhumane acts that the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the accused knew of the beatings and by failing to take any appropriate measures which he as the warden as obliged to adopt, he encouraged these acts at least in respect of his subordinates, and on that basis they were satisfied that his liability for, in this case, aiding and abetting the beatings pursuant to 7(1) was established. That would equally be applicable here. However, we also accept that the Trial Chamber has room to manoeuvre, as it were, discretion as to finding the appropriate classification to describe best a person's criminal responsibility, and here the Trial Chamber decided that on this particular facts of the beatings being done by the guards and the guards in conjunction with the outsiders coming in, that the more appropriate basis of his liability is to think about it under 7(3), and for that reason we confined our appeal ground basically to that finding of the Trial Chamber's judgement. But there's definitely equally no other -- he could just as equally be convicted under a 7(3) mode of liability. You're quite right. Thank you, Your Honours. If there is no further questions on that ground, I'll proceed to my next ground, which is the fifth ground of appeal, persecution based on beatings. It's our submission that it was wholly unreasonable of the Trial Chamber to find that out of the multitude of beatings in the KP Dom, over 50 to 60 beatings which were established on the evidence, that only two of these amounted to persecution. And in our submission, the Trial Chamber failed to draw the only rational and reasonable inference available from the evidence as to the discriminatory nature or grounds of these beatings, and it was simply wrong of the Trial Chamber to not consider the evidence proving the overwhelmingly discriminatory prison setup. This was a prison set up systematically discriminatory environment which pervaded every aspect of the detainees' lives, from the initial imprisonment, why they were there, through to their inhumane conditions, how they had to live, down to the rules imposed upon them, very strict rules governing their lives in the KP Dom. In effect, Your Honours, what the Trial Chamber did was to divorce the evidence on beatings from the surrounding evidence of the discriminatory system in which they took place and then to sort of artificially, after compartmentalising the evidence on the beating, analyse each one in turn. Just to make it very clear, the error I'm speaking about actually effects all the beatings in the KP Dom, but for this, for the purposes of this appeal, we've restricted the impact of the error to those beatings which rose to cruel treatment, inhumane acts, and the conduct is not already covered in our torture ground. And this leaves a sizable number of beatings, almost 40 beatings, to be included in the persecution count under Article 7(3). We're talking here about the Trial Chamber's error in failing to find that the actual assailants, the actual beaters, acted with the requisite discriminatory innocent. And, Your Honours, this is a very or most curious finding. The Trial Chamber made extensive findings on the deliberately discriminatory nature of the imprisonment. They were there because they were Muslims or non-Serbs. And the deliberately discriminatory nature of the inhumane conditions under which they were detained. Take a look at paragraphs 438, 440, 443 of the judgement for those findings. Indeed, for every aspect of what the detainees had to endure while they were in KP Dom, the lack of food, the lack of heat, the lack of adequate clothing, lack of access to medicine, the rules, well, here the Trial Chamber was prepared to accept that they were carried out with the intent to discriminate on religious or political grounds and they were persecutory, but not the beatings. And for these, what the Trial Chamber has done is to positively reject evidence of the discriminatory context in which the beatings occurred as evidence from which inferences can be made as to the discriminatory nature of the beatings, and we see this most clearly in paragraphs 436 and 437, and footnote 1345. So having taken this rejection of the context, this more or less boxed in the Trial Chamber and forced it into a virtual corner. It had to then look at all the evidence on the beatings and specifically look for evidence that the beater at the time of beating sort of verbally expressed or did something overt to express his intentions. And if they didn't find that evidence, then there was no discriminatory grounds established. Your Honours, we can well understand the Trial Chamber placing some limits on inferring the discriminatory nature of an attack simply because it's happening in the process of a wider discriminatory attack. But it's an entirely different matter when the beatings themselves are so very proximate to the discriminatory context of the criminal enterprise. I'd like to think of the KP Dom being almost like a confined discriminatory bubble in which all this activity is going on. We're not talking about drawing inferences from what's going on in Foca, the wider attack, the discriminatory of what's going on in the wider town and municipality. We're talking about drawing natural inferences from the very place, the very system in which these were a fundamental, integral feature of this systematically discriminatory place. In this context, it was utterly unreasonable to separate the acts of beatings from their context. The beatings were as much a part of the system of discriminatory treatment at KP Dom as the shocking living conditions such as no -- the lack of food and the lack of heat and the cramped cells. They're integral. So how can all aspects of their terrible living conditions be discriminatory but not the beatings which, after all, is just another way, another form of breaking down the detainees' mind and body? We, in this respect, would follow the approach in the Kvocka judgement, the Tadic Trial Chamber has taken this approach. Jelisic Trial Chamber took this approach in -- for genocide. Even the Trial Chamber in Kordic. Absent evidence to the contrary, in an environment like KP Dom's, which is overwhelmingly, persistently, systematically discriminatory, an evidentiary presumption must arise that for acts committed in furtherance of that system, such as the beatings, these were also carried out with an intend to perpetuate that discrimination. Of course, we recognise there is a possibility that there may be another reason, another reason which completely overrides the discriminatory reason for a particular beating. In that case, then the Prosecution would have to obviously discount that to the relevant burden -- to the relevant standard, and the Prosecution always bears the burden of proof in this respect. We would submit that this approach of drawing the only rational and natural inferences from the close, very close environment in which they took place is far safer than relying on express statements of intention merely because a beater happened to verbalise his intention and the victim remembered it as well. So what are we saying, that well, if a beater is silent or if the beater beats the victim to such a pulp that the victim doesn't remember anything being said because he lost all consciousness during most of it, then, what, that is not going to be -- well, we're not going to have evidence of persecution in that sort of situation if we're always looking for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- discriminatory intent. Again, I, in the interests of time, will refer you to the examples in the brief relating to Dzemo Balic and Witness 3, FWS-3, to show you that this kind of approach is really, with respect, absurd. What's the only reasonable conclusion? That all beatings in KP Dom were carried out on discriminatory grounds, even those which were done for a confession or to get a confession or for punishment. In this case, in the case of -- if there was another intention there like punishment, then the beater is acting more or less with a mixture of intentions, and I think it would be disingenuous not to recognise the most obvious one, that is discrimination on religious or political grounds even if the information -- even if the evidence also shows he intended to get information or to intimidate or even if there was a personal reason mixed up in that mind. As we know, the discriminatory intent need only be a significant one and not the sole or dominant one. Your Honours, I have one very brief final submission I would like to make on this ground, and that just -- that concerns the requirement in the actus reus, the Trial Chamber's interposition of a legal requirement that in order to show that discrimination in fact has occurred, the victim must objectively belong to the racial, religious, or political group being persecuted. So the Trial Chamber's group regarding discriminatory -- the Trial Chamber's test on discriminatory consequences wouldn't include, for example, sympathisers of the group or people who were actually mistaken as being members and turned out not, to objectively bear those criteria. It is not strictly necessary for this appeal to specifically address this issue since here all the victims of the beatings are objectively members of the targeted group, i.e., non-Serbs and specifically in relation to beatings they're all Muslim. So that extra -- even if that test exists, the extra element is met here on these facts. But we do reject this extra legal element in the definition of persecution, this requirement in the actus reus, and we follow -- we adopt the judgement in Kvocka on this issue at paragraph 195, and Tuta, Stela at paragraphs 636, and Blaskic and Tadic Trial Chambers. The question of whether discrimination in fact has occurred must be looked at from the point of view of the perpetrator. That is, victims are discriminated in fact when targeted for who are what they are perceived to be by the perpetrator. And in our view, this is the only view which accords with the social value protected by the crime of persecution which is aimed at protecting certain groups and their members from harm. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions, and if I can be of further assistance. Your Honour, if there are no questions, I would like to introduce the -- my next speaker, Ms. Norul Rashid, who will speak to you on two grounds of appeal, grounds 6 and 7, on deportation and forced transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to make up some of the time we -- we are missing, I suggest that we go until 10.50. That will give about an hour and a half to the Prosecution to express -- to put forward its arguments. So we will go on for about another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I will use up the next 15 minutes allocated to me to submit, to make submissions on the seventh ground of appeal. I will start with that first and then I'll move on to the sixth ground of appeal. Your Honour, the respondent was charged under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Not 15 minutes, no, no. But we'll take a break in 15 minutes. But of course the Prosecutor still has time after the break, another hour. So you can organise yourself accordingly. But we'll take our break ten of. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour. He was charged and acquitted of deportation and expulsion of Muslim and other non-Serb civilians detained in the KP Dom facility, to Montenegro and other places which are unknown. And this has been charged as persecution under count 1 of the indictment. Your Honours, in this ground of appeal, it is our contention that the Trial Chamber erred in its findings on deportation and expulsion as persecution. We have raised in our appeal brief five specific errors of law and fact, and that has been -- and they have been comprehensively addressed. For purposes of this hearing and in view of the time allocated, I propose to address the first limb of this ground of appeal. Your Honour, we submit that the Trial Chamber erred in law in holding that the acts of forcible displacement charged as persecution require proof that the victims were forcibly displaced across a national border and that deportation is to be distinguished from forcible transfer which may take place within national boundaries. The Trial Chamber was in fact satisfied that the majority of the incidents alleged by the Prosecution in Annex 4 of the indictment do constitute deportation and expulsion did take place. These incidents may be divided into categories; transfer of detainees to other prison camps, so-called exchanges, and so-called work duty outside the KP Dom which some of the detainees were performing. It is the Prosecution's principal submission that deportation under Article 5 of the Statute and the act of expulsion include not only unlawful displacements across a national boundary but also unlawful displacements within a state's national boundaries. The provisions of international law, Your Honour, regulating international armed conflicts should not limit the prohibition against deportations as a crime against humanity under Article 5 to cross-border transfers. In this context, deportation should be viewed as an umbrella term encompassing acts of forcible displacement whether internal or cross a border. There are just three points I wish to highlight for Your Honours' consideration. First, we submit that the key in attempting to define the scope and content of deportation as a crime against humanity lies in identifying the interests or the harm that it seeks to protect. The primary harm protected by the prohibition of deportation in contemporary international law must be the unjustified interference with the right of individuals to remain in their homes and in their communities. Undoubtedly, the immediate consequences of unlawful displacement usually constitute violations of basic human rights. In the context of human rights law, displacement threatens the life, the liberty, and the security of the displaced, rights which are guaranteed, for instance, in Article 3 of the Universal Declaration, Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Freedom of movement is inherently breached when displacement occurs not only because the displaced are invariably restricted - for instance, some of them may end up in detention camps - but also because they cannot exercise their right to return to their home country or principal area. The Trial Chamber in Krstic, at paragraph 523 of the judgement, for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker speak a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: My apologies to the translators, Your Honour. I'll slow down. -- for instance, noted that any forced displacement is by definition a traumatic experience which involves abandoning one's home, losing property, and being displaced under duress to another location. If we go back in time, it must be recalled, for instance, that during the First World War, the German deportation and population transfer were for very specific purposes. They were for purposes of subjecting the people to extermination, slavery, and forced labour in accordance with the final solution, regardless of whether the Nuremberg accused were indicted for deportation for purposes of forced labour, a war crime, or deportation simpliciter, crimes against humanity. In the context of the former Yugoslavia, it is pertinent to recall, Your Honour, very briefly the final report of the commission of experts, page 33 which define ethnic cleansing in these terms. Considered in the context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia means rendering an area ethnically homogenous by using force or intimidation to remove persons of given groups from the area, carried out by various means which include forcible removal, displacement, and deportation of civilian population. Ahmici, April 1993. The Kupreskic Trial Chamber found, at paragraph 760 to 762 of the trial judgement that the attack on Ahmici as part of an overall campaign in the Lasva River Valley was intended to bring about ethnic cleansing through a systematic and widespread attack. The reason for the forced expulsion, according to the Trial Chamber, was the achievement of territorial homogeneity by the Croats. The aim of the attack was the forced expulsion of the Muslim population from the area, as from the entire Lasva River valley. Srebrenica, July 1995. The Krstic Trial Chamber found that the transfer of civilians from Srebrenica enclave was carried out in furtherance of a well-organised policy whose purpose was to expel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please slow down her reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: -- whose purpose was to expel the Bosnian Muslim population from the enclave. According to the Trial Chamber, evacuation itself was the goal. Krstic was found guilty of forcible transfer under Article 5. Foca 1992 to 1995. In this case, the cleansing of Foca was achieved through various means. The end result was one; the forced removal of an ethnic group and eviction from their ordinary places of residence. In this context, the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 49 of the judgement which has been alluded to by my colleague Mr. Staker, that in late 1994, the last remaining Muslim detainees at KP Dom were exchanged, marking the achievement of a Serbian region ethnically cleansed of Muslims. By the end of 1994, Foca was almost purely a Serb town. The Trial Chamber has essentially accepted that the exchanges that occurred at KP Dom were in fact part of the ethnic cleansing policy practised in Foca between 1992 to 1995.
