Your Honour, what this demonstrates is simply this: The focus of deportation as a crime against humanity is, A, the very act of removal and the consequences on the victims; and B, the goal that the perpetrator seeks to achieve by the acts of removal. The final destination of the victims in this situation is inconsequential. The second point that I wish to make is that there is compelling -- compelling evidence by way of opinion juris that deportation and forcible transfer are synonymous. They're synonymous terms. There have been very little attempts, Your Honours, in international instruments to fully delineate the distinctions between the term deportation and other crimes described as forcible transfer and unlawful transfer. The Appeals Chamber must seize this opportunity to try and resolve this issue, because even at the trial level, the position is still unclear. The Prosecutor submits that the ICC Statute, the Rome Statute is a significant turning point rejecting a restricted reading of the crime of deportation. I refer Your Honours to Article 7(1), to (d), which defines the term deportation or forcible transfer conjunctively defined as: "The forced displacement of the persons concerned, by expulsion or other coercive acts from the area in which they are lawfully present without grounds permitted under international law." And the footnote pertaining to this provision provides that, "deported or forcibly transferred is interchangeable with forcibly displaced." Eighty-nine states have ratified the statute. Australia, Canada, Malta, Estonia, New Zealand, South Africa, UK have all enacted legislation substantially adopting the definition of deportation as set out in Article 7. The conflict in East Timor, Your Honours, section 5.1(d), regulation 2015 lists deportation or forcible transfer of population as crimes against humanity. The text from the regulation is a direct adoption of the ICC Statute. There is a judgement that I wish to refer Your Honour to from the East Timor War Crimes Tribunal, and I have included that in the supplemental book of authorities, Your Honour. In this case, four of the 11 accused were charged with deportation or forcible transportation of population to places within East Timor and across to West Timor. No distinction was drawn between the civilians who ended up in East Timor and those who ended up in West Timor. No distinction was made between the terms deportation and forcible transfer. In their judgement, the panel knows that there was a lack of definition of the requisite elements for the crime of deportation or forcible transfer, but accepted that the rules, the rules of the then-draft ICC Statute, which it noted was substantially grounded on the Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Convention. There is also another case which I have included in the supplemental book of authorities, which is the case of Andrija Artukovic, a District Court in Zagreb case. The defendant was convicted among other crimes for the arrest and deportation of a victim to a concentration camp in Danica within -- this camp was within the territory of the former Yugoslavia. We submit, Your Honour, that the Blaskic Trial Chamber correctly relied on the ICC Statute at paragraph 418 of the judgement whereby it adopted and accepted the definition set out in Article 7(2)(d). The third point that I wish to make is that there is simply no justification to retain the additional element which the Trial Chamber said exist for the crime of deportation. There is no justification to be found either in customary or contemporary international law for deportation to be read this way. There are, in fact, sound policy justifications permitting a broader reading of deportation as a crime against humanity under Article 5(d). Both forcible transfers and deportations are still crimes against humanity under Article 5. There is no hierarchy in terms of the gravity of all these crimes both internal and cross-border transfers are proscribed under customary international law. For example, Article 17 of the Additional Protocol II, it covers both internal and external transfers. There is, therefore, no suggestion that deportation is more grave requiring an additional element or -- of border crossing. The Rome Statute also -- the Rome Statute's definition accords with the realities of contemporary armed conflicts where it might be difficult at any given point in time to specify the exact borders of a country in conflict. The situation in East and West Timor is an example. Contemporary conflicts, Your Honour, we've moved away from the Nuremberg situations where there was thousands of transfers from Germany to other places, and we have moved towards civil or internal conflicts. The Trial Chamber, therefore, was essential -- was wrong to have essentially concluded that deportation means a definite and direct act of removal, putting people on buses and requiring the Prosecution to trace the journey of these victims to the border of the state and requiring the Prosecution to prove that each and every detainee was dispatched nowhere else but across the border. Forced displacement can also be practiced in a more indirect, less organised manner. This type of displacement can occur in a region where armed conflict is ongoing or where systematic human rights violations are being committed. It is sometimes factored, as the Trial Chamber has knowledge in this case, under the pretext of an exchange. It is irrelevant under which factual veil a person is being displaced. Criminal liability attaches once removal is effected no matter which matters are being used to achieve the goal. The final destination of the victims in this case, be it a mass grave at the Gorazde front line in Bosnia-Herzegovina for at least two of the detainees, the 20 men supposedly taken for exchange and simply disappeared, the 35 men who were eventually --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: -- Montenegro, Your Honour. The final destination cannot be an element of the crime. For all these detainees, they could never return to their lawful places of residence. For all these detainees, they were effectively and, in fact, deported from Foca. Your Honour, determining the accused's responsibility under Article 7(1) as an aider and abettor or co-perpetrator, it must be shown that the accused was aware that the perpetrators forcibly removed the detainees. The facts or circumstances established the lawfulness or the presence of the persons deported and he must have been aware that they were carried out on discriminatory grounds. I can do no better than refer the Court to the facts and the evidence set out in the appeal brief the -- to show that the accused did in fact know that the Muslim detainees at KP Dom were being exchanged as part of an elaborate exchange programme. He was aware of that fact. He knew that during the 15 months as KP Dom warden, under his direct supervision these detainees were being allegedly exchanged. He was perfectly aware of the fate of these detainees, and I have outlined the submissions in my appeal brief, Your Honour. That concludes the submissions on the seventh ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I think that you should then speak about the sixth ground of appeal, and I suggest that we take a break and that we resume at 11.30. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. Before we move to further argument of the Prosecution, I think that Judge Schomburg would like to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Not to be misunderstood, especially not by the Defence, with the question of deportation opposed to forcible transfer, we are entering a new terrain, and the jurisprudence no doubt is not settled and, therefore, we have to decide on this and therefore, the question is at the same time directed to the Defence. I must admit that I'm satisfied and appreciate that in this case the Prosecution did not plead forcible transfer as another inhumane act. We have to take this into account. It is mentioned in the judgement, in the Trial Chamber's judgement, that this was not pleaded and, therefore, there is an obstacle to include this. Why do I appreciate this? Because I believe the notion of other inhumane act is to a certain extent conflicting with the principle nullem crimen sine lege, especially here. We don't have a precise enough description of the crime and of the offence. Therefore, I think the right way is in fact to put the question whether or not we have an act of deportation before us. Your fundamental first observation is the following; that you say all forcible displacements would amount to deportation. In your own description, I can follow your line of arguments in as far as you state that in the alternative - and this is paragraph 817 of your arguments - that deportation, the appropriate interpretation of the word "deportation" would be were expelled by a belligerent party from the territory held by that party regardless of whether the boundary concerned is internationally recognised or not. I think it would be only consequent under Article 5 to come closer with -- to this solution because we should be aware that the jurisprudence in its entirety has changed, and we have a case before us where we discuss internal, an internal armed conflict, and therefore, the question before us is -- in fact wouldn't be appropriate to consequently state that when a person is brought from an area of sovereignty or power to another area of power, that this could be and should be called deportation. You made reference to the English notion of deportation. I think here we don't have a language problem because deportation/deportation, we have the same notion in all our languages. And the Latin root of this word, in my mind, is from one part to the other, in the meaning of you are in a safe harbour and you are not allowed to stay in this safe harbour. But then my question would be: What is, in your mind, opposed to deportation, expulsion? Isn't it the same? Just forcing a person to leave the area of power. My question, in addition, would be: If we would endorse your first line of arguments, what would be the limitation? Would it be enough to bring a person from one house to the next house? Would this be already deportation? What about these internal forcible transfers in one area of power or sovereignty? Could this really amount to deportation or wouldn't this be in fact forcible transfer? And we should be aware that forcible -- aware forcible transfer is, as I said, in my opinion not covered by other inhumane acts. And in addition, we have in our Statute some rules on forcible transfer in other cases. Therefore, one could arguably state that this forcible transfer within the area of power does not amount to deportation. That is the first question, the first part of the question. The second is: What about the voluntary aspect of the deportation related to those persons brought to Montenegro? Here I think we have an additional problem. It is your submission that in this case the exchange amounts to deportation, but my question is: Isn't it a fundamental principle of rule when you allege a person to have committed a crime that there must be an alternative that is not punishable, and wouldn't this be the case if you would say that they shouldn't have done this exchange, but what would be the alternative, to keep these persons imprisoned? Wouldn't it be the argument then by the Prosecution to state they committed continuously this crime of deprivation of liberty for political and ethnic reasons? I would appreciate if you could give some comments on these two -- on this twofold question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with regard to your first question regarding expulsion and deportation, we have charged under Count 1 deportation and expulsion as opposed to recent cases where we have charged it as deportation and forcible transfer. There is a difference in the charging practices on the part of the Prosecution. The argument that we made with regard to expulsion is that it is a generic term. It is not a technical term. It's not to be found anywhere in the Statute or international instruments. It's not a specific crime. It has been used by the Prosecution and by the Prosecution in the Kupreskic indictment. We have secured a conviction for that particular act, expulsion as a persecutory act. It has been used to describe a persecutory conduct whereby it denotes an attempt or act of forcibly removing the victims from one place. That is the basic layman's meaning of expulsion, but seen in the context of persecution, it is merely used to define the process by which a person has been removed from an area which is by force or coercive acts, so it is not really a crime as such. It is quite distinct from deportation. Deportation has been given a legal definition by this Tribunal as well as by reference to the ICC Statute, but the end result and the content of these two acts, we're basically describing the same conduct here. The terms -- the terms -- the terms used are different, the words used are different; it's a matter of labelling. And it is, at the end of the day, a language trap because we are talking about the same conduct; external and internal transfers. And there is nothing in customary international law or contemporary international law that has drawn any significant distinction between all these terms: "Unlawful transfer," "forcible displacement," "forcible transfer," "expulsion," and we are now submitting "deportation." It is just a matter of labelling. With regard to the second part of Your Honour's question, forcible transfer, whether it is possible to effect forcible transfer from one area to another area occupied by -- by the opposing forces, our submission is that yes, it is an alternative argument to our first, main principal argument on deportation. If at all, under Article 5 which describes -- which is a crime against humanity and applies to an armed conflict which may not be characterised as international or internal, if we take the view that you need a specific border crossing that is across another country, you can never charge an individual for deportation as crimes against humanity under Article 5(d). This cannot be the situation contemplated either in the Nuremberg Charter or under the Statute. Both -- all forms of transfers are prohibited under customary international law. The scaled down borders that we have advanced, that we have proposed reflects the reality of what is going on in the internal conflicts around the world today. The former Yugoslavia, for instance, where the entire conflict was about territorial disputes. The conflict in East Timor, for instance. So, yes, that scaled-down version of a border we have proposed and which we say is still legal under customary international law because the basis for that assertion is that all forms of transfers are prohibited under international law. We do not think that this offends the principle of nullem crimen sine lege. Forcible transfer, I do agree with Your Honour it is not listed anywhere in the Statute. It is listed in Article 4, forcible transfer of children as a genocidal act, yes, that's true. The Trial Chambers have, however, at least in two Trial Chambers, Krstic and the recent Tuta and Stela judgements, have decided that forcible transfer could constitute a crime against humanity either under persecution or inhumane treatment, 5(i). And I do understand -- of course I do realise that in Stakic the Trial Chamber has expressed reservations on that issue. But forcible transfer is not really an issue for purposes of this appeal. The definition or -- as to whether forcible transfer on its own could constitute an inhumane treatment is not really an issue on this appeal, which is why we have not really addressed these substantively in our appeal. But if we do have to take a position, then I would adopt the position we took in the Stakic closing brief, the Prosecution final closing brief. We have addressed Your Honour's concerns extensively in the brief. Your Honour, with regard to the voluntary aspect of deportation, Your Honour has asked whether there is an alternative to the conduct that we have ascribed to the accused as a crime, a conduct which is not punishable. It's an interesting question. It's a difficult question. Exchanges usually happen in internal conflicts, in conflicts. They're not really crimes. They have not been listed as crimes either under Geneva law or in the Additional Protocols, they're certainly not listed as a crime under the Statute. But on the facts of this case, and I say this is a factual issue, the Trial Chamber has found that these so-called exchanges, and they refer to them as so-called exchanges because the Trial Chamber accepted that they were bogus, that these were not really exchanges. If you look at the evidence we have outlined in the brief, some of the guards told the detainees, "Don't go. Don't volunteer to be exchanged," because they knew that these exchanges were in fact an attempt to deport or remove the individuals from KP Dom, and that is part of the -- and that is one of the means whereby detainees were actually removed from KP Dom. The alternative on the facts of this case is simply not viable. Most of the men disappeared. Two of them were found dead in a mass grave. Some of them were actually deported across the border, but on the facts of this case, it's very clear from the judgement that the Court accepted that they weren't really exchanged. Is exchange a viable option? Yes, if it's genuine and if it ensures the safety of the detainees. And why do we say the accused is liable for these crimes is because he did not take any measures to ensure that the detainees were in fact lawfully or legally exchanged. We have set out in the submission that he knew that there were problems with these exchanges. There were problems transporting the detainees. I hope I have answered your second question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would just add a further point in response to your question, the one in relation to whether there must be a viable alternative in order for conduct to be held criminal. We would also submit that it's a general proposition that if a person deprives themselves from any alternative by committing a crime, they cannot rely on their own crime as a defence to a subsequent crime which deprived them of that alternative. If the criminal act consists in unlawfully detaining civilians, you cannot plead that crime as a defence to their transfer by saying that what choice did we have? Having unlawfully confined them, what else could we do with them? But in any case there was a simple answer: It would have been to release them to return to their homes in Foca. Again it's not a defence. It's not a defence to that to say yes, but we were conducting a persecutory campaign in Foca and therefore it wasn't safe for them to return to their homes. Because the submission I made earlier was that there was a single joint criminal enterprise, and you cannot plead as a defence to one part of the enterprise some other part of the same criminal enterprise. On the question of whether prisoner exchanges can ever be lawful, in our submission, that question doesn't arise in this case, and it may be undesirable for it to be addressed for the reason that the Trial Chamber made the findings in paragraph 49 of the trial judgement that the expulsion, exchange, or deportation of non-Serbs was the final stage of the Serb attack upon the non-Serb civilian population in Foca municipality. I referred to this paragraph earlier in my own submissions. At the end of that paragraph it says: "Late in 1994, the last remaining Muslim detainees at the KP Dom were exchanged." The word "exchange" is used. "Marking the end of the attack upon those civilians and the achievement of a Serbian region, ethnically cleansed of Muslims." In our submission, the question whether an exchange could ever be lawful does not arise. This exchange was part of the joint criminal enterprise, and in our submission, that would answer the question about viable alternatives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Rashid, I was interested in my colleague Judge Schomburg's question to you as to the limits of your thesis. He asked if there was an expulsion of a family from one house to another house, would that be deportation? Now, that has led me to think of this, and I say to you that I may well have been at fault in overlooking something in your writings which bore upon this question, but your reference to Article 5(d) of the Statute refreshes my thinking on the subject, and what I want to put to you is this: Are you inviting the Bench to draw in implications from the chapeau of Article 5? We all know that an armed conflict is not necessary under customary international law for the constitution of a crime against humanity, but it has been put in here by the Security Council. Now, what are the implications of that? Should we say that the chapeau of Article 5 necessarily implies that all the legal ingredients of a crime of deportation can be realised in the course of an internal armed conflict, that all the legal ingredients of an act of deportation can occur in the course of an internal armed conflict? If that is true, does it have a bearing on the question as to whether the deportation being instanced there necessary states a cross-border, international border transfer or does it imply that the deportation can well incur purely internally, because the statute says -- speaks of crimes when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal. Can you help me on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: I most certainly can. Sorry, Your Honour. I most certainly can help you on that. That is the thrust of our argument. Article -- deportation is listed as a crime against humanity. The requirements of a -- of deportation as a crime against humanity with regard to the chapeau, yes, you do need an armed conflict, but you do not need to characterise the armed conflict. All you need to show is the widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population. Of course it is beyond -- without doubt that crimes against humanity can occur in internal -- applies to internal armed conflict as well as external armed conflict. And that has been the thrust of our argument, Your Honour, that according to the statute, crimes against humanity must be committed in armed conflict, but the nature is completely immaterial. The provisions of international law regulating international armed conflict should not limit the prohibitions against deportations as crimes against humanity to cross-border transfers. It should not because of the nature and the way we have interpreted Article 5 as applying to internal armed conflict, which is why we submitted in the appeal brief that deportation should carry this umbrella term and should cover internal and external and cross-border transfers as well. So yes, I completely agree with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Rashid, it remains for me to apologise very deeply to you in case I overlooked something in your appeal brief which said what I was proposing to you, that the chapeau of Article 5 necessarily implies that all legal ingredients of an act of deportation may occur internally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: If Your Honour is referring to paragraph 8.7 of our appeal brief, then that is the thrust of our argument, Your Honour, is the characterisation of the armed conflict issue. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a clarification that I'd like to ask for.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I'm wondering whether you do make a distinction between expulsion and deportation. Do you make a distinction in terms of criminal law?

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: No. The way deportation and expulsion has been charged as a singular conduct, it describes the same conduct. Deportation includes external transfers. Expulsion basically describes the same conduct. I have submitted earlier, Your Honour, that expulsion is to describe a process by which a person has been removed. It has been categorised as a persecutory act. Persecution is not defined in terms of the conduct constituting persecution, so expulsion becomes a crime -- becomes a persecutory crime if it fulfils all the requirements of persecution. And that is how we have charged it in this case. Is there a difference in terms of substance and content and scope? No, Your Honour. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish my comment, please. You should be careful about one thing. I'm sure that you're paying close attention to your case, but I think that expulsion that is similar to deportation is when we're talking about there is an armed conflict. But let me remind you - and Judge Schomburg already said this - that deportation has to do with international law or international -- national or international law, it's always a crime, whether linguistically that is used in French or in English. Deportation means that one deports prisoners, but they are -- these give rise to crimes, whereas expulsion can be an act of sovereignty. I could tell you that every day governments expel certain categories of population that, for instance, do not satisfy the legal conditions for entering a territory. You do know that. One can expel but one expels because that is sovereignty just as one could expel oneself because one is trying to prevent people from coming in, whereas deportation is completely different. I can understand that you make no distinction between the two terms, but if you don't, then you're including expulsion and saying that it is the same as deportation because, as in this case, for instance, we would then be allegedly dealing with a joint criminal enterprise which is part of an international armed conflict. So then I do understand that the distinction would be much less clear. I just wanted to make this clarification. Judge Schomburg, I believe, wished to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, it would be just a follow-up question to this. If one, for instance, would endorse your alternative as outlined in paragraph 817 and accept that this would be a valid interpretation of the phrase and the notion of deportation, what would be opposed to this, the added criminal behaviour not yet included in deportation, but you need to make reference in addition to expulsion. I think what -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: With regard to expulsion, and I just wish to clarify this in light of the President's comments, expulsion has not been listed as a crime. It's not -- there are no elements to the term "expulsion." That much is clear. We have charged to describe a conduct which we say amounts to a persecutory act. It is not a technical term that we are using in the sense that the President has outlined. Yes, I do agree with Your Honour, of course, that expulsion carries all these various other meanings, but charged in the context of persecution and described in the indictment as a persecutory act, that becomes a crime of persecution. There is no added element as such. The Court can look at expulsion in isolation from deportation which I agree holds a more technical meaning. Yes, of course. But we have emphasised in the appeal brief that expulsion is actually a generic term and is merely used to describe a specific conduct. There are no elements to the crime of expulsion, for instance. You look for elements. You look at the elements of persecution to see whether that act actually amounts to a crime of persecution. Your Honour, I hope I have clarified that, our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I will take about ten, maybe ten minutes to go through the ground 6, and I will keep it brief. Your Honours, in this ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the labour of at least eight of the detainees that we have listed in the appeal brief was involuntary or that it constituted forced labour under the law. As a result, the Trial Chamber committed, we claim, a series of errors resulting in the acquittal of the accused for the crime of forced labour charged as a persecutory act under Article 5(H). Your Honour, in our appeal brief, we have asked you to consider our two related arguments. The first argument relates to the erroneous application of the law of consent to the facts of the case. The second argument which we have raised relates to the status of unlawfully detained, protected persons and whether Article 5.1 of the Additional Protocol II applies to these individuals. I would request that you view the second argument from the perspective of determining a consent, and I propose to address the first argument first as I intend to develop it further. The Trial Chamber at paragraph 360 of the judgement relied -- held that civilians deprived of their liberty in the context of a non-international armed conflict can nevertheless be made to work under certain circumstances. The sole reference is -- in support is Article 5.1 of Additional Protocol II. The Prosecution invites the Appeals Chamber to consider as a matter of legal significance whether paragraph 5(e) of Additional Protocol II is applicable to the very different circumstances of persons unlawfully detained as part of a persecutory campaign on the basis of their religion or politics. It is the Prosecution's contention, after having reviewed the Geneva law and Additional Protocol II, that it does not. Persons unlawfully deprived of their liberty cannot be compelled to work. The Trial Chamber, Your Honour, although correctly viewed the provision from the perspective of consent nonetheless required evidence, for instance, of the nature of work and the conditions of work and rejected much of the evidence due to absence of such evidence. We did not appeal this issue specifically because we did not rely on it at trial but we seek your guidance on this issue: Do provisions in the Geneva Conventions and Protocols compelling protected persons to work apply to unlawfully detained protected persons? Your Honour, very briefly, and I have more or less outlined the submissions in my appeal brief, the Prosecution submits that neither the provisions in the four Geneva Conventions nor those in Additional Protocol II specifically address the permissibility or otherwise of compelling unlawfully detained civilians to perform any kind of work. There are basically two points that I wish to outline with respect to Article 5.1. Article 5.1 refers to persons whose liberty has been restricted which we submit refers to permissible forms of detention made lawful under international law. The second element to Article 5.1(e) talk about the benefits of working conditions and safeguards accorded to these individuals made to perform labour. In this regard, I would request that Your Honour look at Article 95 of Geneva Convention IV; Article 40, 41 of Geneva Convention IV; Articles 79, 41 to 43, 68 and 78 of the Geneva Convention IV, which all make references to detainees, internees and persons placed under assigned residences, lawfully detained individuals who can be compelled to work under certain circumstances if certain conditions are fulfilled. I would also refer Your Honour to the commentary to Additional Protocol II, which basically states that the term "deprived of their liberty for reasons related to the armed conflict" covers persons penally prosecuted and those deprived of their liberty for security reasons. Similar reasons as to why persons may be detained, the circumstances under which persons may be detained under Geneva law. Your Honour, the general rule is that a civilian cannot be arbitrarily deprived of his liberty. That would be tantamount to unlawful confinement or imprisonment. Considering the limited circumstances under which a civilian may be detained due to reasons of the armed conflict, it follows that it is only in exceptional circumstances that a civilian may be compelled to work if certain conditions are fulfilled. We submit that the exceptional circumstances do not arise if the general rule is breached, as it was in this case, and I refer Your Honour to paragraph 122 of the judgement. I would also ask that Your Honour look at the rationale for compelling protected persons to work. I make reference to Article 8 of the 1966 International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights which list the form of permissible forced labour. I would also make reference to the commentary on Article 5 which talks about the reasons why work -- why a person deprived of his liberty may be compelled to work under certain circumstances. The Tuta and Stela judgement, at paragraph 253, also explored the reasons as to why a prisoner of war should be or can be made to work. I do not propose to go through, Your Honour, the judgement, but it's instructive. The normal work conditions contemplated under Article 5.1 are not compatible in my submission with camp cases such as this one because it is highly unlikely that these safeguards, the protections accorded to under Geneva law or the Additional Protocols, would and could apply to detainees held under KP Dom circumstances. Detainees unlawfully arrested, imprisoned, and held in inhumane conditions. If the argument is made on the facts that it was in the interests of the detainees or it benefited them in some way, the facts show otherwise, and these have been outlined in my brief as well. Your Honour, there are no provisions either in Geneva law or in protocols compelling unlawfully detained protected persons to work. The nature of the work performed, for example, those listed in Article 50 of Geneva Convention III, which is the litmus test in determining whether a protected individual can be compelled to work. It is on this premise that the issue of consent should be viewed in all cases of forced labour. Your Honour, with regard to the second argument, I would ask that your -- the Appeals Chamber review the Trial Chamber's application of the law on consent which we -- which they have correctly set out in paragraph 359 of the judgement to the facts. A couple of points I wish to make in relation to the objective and subjective criteria in determining consent. Your Honour, it is our submission that even in the absence of evidence from the detainees on the issue of consent, the Trial Chamber should have examined other objective criteria. The emphasis is whether detainees had a real choice. It's distinct and different from the issue of whether the detainees volunteered to work or agreed to work. In ascertaining real choice, the Trial Chamber should have gone beyond what the detainees said, what they did, and examined the detainees' motivations which in this case -- in this case the motivations are also corroborated by the objective coercive circumstances. What does real choice mean, Your Honour? Very briefly, it can be summed up by reference to the testimony of one of the witnesses. This is trial transcript 4860. He said: "Well, perhaps you can call it voluntary in a sense, but I would like to define that sense. If you are locked up in an area out of which you cannot get out at all and if somebody offers you work, then it's always better for you to get outside and work because you can expect to get some things like food, cigarettes, even contacts with Serbs and find out something. It's better than staying in the room. So in a way, you can call it voluntary. Although in another sense, it is quite ridiculous." The Trial Chamber's conclusion that this constitutes voluntary labour or that this witness had agreed to work is simply wrong. Similar evidence was presented by other detainees, and we have set out in the appeal brief, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber's systematic and erroneous misapplication of the law on consent to the facts. Your Honour, I can do no better than refer the Court to my appeal brief for the rest of the grounds, but I will respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber's conclusion and verdict in acquitting the respondent of forced labour has occasioned a serious miscarriage of justice and it must be reversed. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Your Honours, I will be dealing with the fourth ground of appeal. This is in relation to the murders. The Prosecution's fourth ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber committed an error of fact by concluding that for the purposes of Article 7(3), the respondent did not have sufficient information to put him on notice that his subordinates were involved in the murder of the detainees listed in Schedule C. This error caused the Trial Chamber to conclude that the respondent was not liable under Article 7(3) for these murders. I think at the onset I should indicate that there were certain general factual findings made by the Trial Chamber in relation to these murders. Twenty-six of the 29 names listed in Schedule C were found to have in fact to have been committed -- the murders were in fact to have been committed in KP Dom. The Court expressed its reservations in relation to the killing of Milo Hodzic, also in relation to Samir or Amir, depending on how his name was interpreted, Mujezinovic, and also in relation to Huso Dzamalija who, in fact, it is alleged committed suicide. It is important, though, that we appreciate what those factual findings were to the extent that they were totally convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that 26 of those 29 names, 26 of these individuals, died in KP Dom as a result of the participation of the guards of the KP Dom and that they in fact did so in collaboration with the acts of the members of the military coming from outside the camp. It is important, however, to look at this particular factual finding against what I would conceive to be the role, function, and position of, in fact, the appellant in the camp. The Trial Chamber's prior findings as to the respondent's position of authority is important, because in fact it does indicate in a very matter of fact way how the chain of information, that would have been made available to the appellant, operated. In paragraphs 96 to 107, they made a firm conclusion -- they came to the firm conclusion that in fact he held the position of warden, that, in fact, the lease agreement did not in any way effect the hierarchical system operating within that prison, and specifically that, in fact, the accused exercised supervisory responsibility over all subordinate personnel and detainees of the KP Dom. They made a reference to FWS-138 who indicated that all in fact the information mechanism procedures that were in place before, before in fact the war, and during -- during that moment of crisis that they essentially remain the same. That in fact, for example, the commander of the guards, Mitar Rasevic, still had to report to in fact Krnojelac. Also for example that Savo Todovic who in fact was the deputy warden had to report to, in fact, Krnojelac. Additionally, that there was a system in place that any kind of alteration or any type of aberration occurring in the camp was subject to a reporting mechanism to the Ministry of Justice. So that to all intents of purposes, when we're trying to determine what in fact would represent sufficient information, that sufficient information must be analysed in the context of the already established chain of information on general and particular issues operating within that particular camp. In so doing, the Trial Chamber concluded that the respondent was a de jure superior of the guards and that, in fact, he failed in his duty to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish the crimes for the following bases: They indicated, and this is at paragraph 107, that he failed to investigate the allegations of beatings when he would inevitably have ascertained the identity of those responsible for many of those beatings. It is trite knowledge in the camp that many of the guards like Matovic, Burilo, all these individuals in fact were part of the KP Dom contingent of guards and they were responsible for a lot of the beatings that were, in fact, taking place. In fact, they also found that the respondent failed to order the guards to stop beating detainees and to take appropriate measures. They found he failed to speak to his subordinates about the mistreatment of detainees. They said he also failed to punish those guards who could easily have been identified and he failed to report these abuses to higher authority. The respondent -- it is important to note that the respondent's position as the warden of KP Dom and his failure to punish crime was reiterated by the Trial Chamber on its discussion of the respondent's liability for murders committed in KP Dom. In relation to the general findings that the Trial Chamber made with regard to his potential responsibility for the murders, it is important to note that they came to various conclusions. One very pivotal conclusion was that they were satisfied that the respondent had knowledge that the detainees were being beaten and were disappearing from the KP Dom during the evenings of June 1992. It was not satisfied, however, that those said detainees, in fact, that were being called out in the evenings and were subsequently disappearing were being killed. In so doing, in fact, they rejected the theory, the 7(1) theory with regard to aiding and abetting even though they appreciated that by his failure in fact to take the appropriate measures, he in fact created an atmosphere, a system whereby in fact these particular crimes could have been committed. But more particularly and relevant to this particular ground of appeal, he rejected the Prosecution's -- the Trial Chamber rejected the Prosecution's theory that the respondent incurred superior responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) for the deaths that occurred in KP Dom during June and July of 1992, although this is in the face of the fact that they recognised that the appellant was quite aware of two deaths in the camp. He was aware of the death of Halim Konjo and he was also aware of the death of Huso Dzamalija, yet they found that, notwithstanding that particular knowledge, it did not represent the sufficiency of knowledge required. The Prosecution submits that that conclusion that the respondent lacked responsibility as a superior under Article 7(3) for the murders committed at KP Dom was an error of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice within the meaning of Article 25.2 of the Statute. The Prosecution submits that on the basis of the Trial Chamber's factual findings, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that he was not criminally responsible under Article 7(3) of the Statute for the murders; that the only conclusion that was reasonably available was that sufficient information was available to the respondent which would have, at a minimum, put him on notice of the risk that murders were being committed by his subordinates. It is important to note that when one looks at the peculiarities of these beatings, the peculiarities of the harsh treatment meted out against these individuals, the only difference between the beatings as found and the murders has to do in terms of what was the inevitable effect. In one case it was a case of beatings that resulted in incapacitation. In another, it was a case of certain beatings that resulted in death. In other words, a level of behaviour, a level of deportment, if I may so describe it, that is of the same genus and of the same type. And significantly, one would consider that when one looks at what in fact is the definition of murder, isn't murder dealing with in fact acts with intent to cause grievous bodily harm? Isn't that what murder is? So does it mean that because, for example, that final step is not reached, that you are not put on inquiry, that there is in fact and indeed a real --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I do apologise. So that when one considers the respondent's position, one can only conclude, having concluded he was a superior of the KP Dom with authority to prevent and punish, and in light of the fact that the Trial Chamber concluded that he had not taken any measure to prevent or punish the beatings inflicted on the non-Serbs, it is our submission that having so found that he had that requisite knowledge in relation to the beatings, it is our humble submission that in fact in relation to the subsequent killings, that there was in fact that sufficient notice. At least, at minimum, it ought to have been in fact put him on inquiry notice. Our submission, as my learned colleague Ms. Brady had indicated to a question by the learned colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, that ours is a case that is based not only on likely-to-know information but more specifically on actual information. When, for example, look -- and I think I may -- it may be pertinent to go into the particular killings at this point in time. You have a situation arising where Huso Dzamalija is alleged to have committed suicide in his cell as a result of beatings, as a result of depression. It is alleged that the Trial Chamber had some doubts as to in fact the real cause of death, whether it was the cause of the beatings or the cause of depression, yet he dies in prison. You have a subsequent killing involving in fact Halil Konjo who in fact RJ speaks to the appellant about at the behest of his brother Halim Konjo. And what he says? He says, Listen, what I want to find out about in fact Halil Konjo. He says, Yes, I know he is dead, and he ends it at that. When, for example, he's pressed in cross-examination and when testifying, what does he say? He says basically I was informed by a nurse, Jankovic, that in fact he died from suicide, he died as a result of suicide. And then Nurse Jankovic, who in fact is, of course, a mere nurse, indicates, well, there was in fact some kind of investigation done into the matter, and he leaves it at that. Here is a situation where you have two deaths of suspicious characteristics. One a suicide, one in fact a death that obviously in fact is extremely suspicious, and in those circumstances the appellant in fact is not put -- is deemed not to have been put on inquiry. I think in fact if we, for example, transpose this to a normal situation, in any normal national jurisdiction, a man dies in prison, whether it be suicide or under suspicious circumstances, all hell will break loose. And we are saying in the circumstances of this particular prison that there was that mechanism, that mechanism for reporting in the system. So in fact he was quite aware that he was in a position to do the necessary inquiry with regard to these killings. We are saying in fact that in those circumstances, the Trial Chamber erred because the only reasonable inference based on those two killings alone against a backdrop of persecutory beatings, against a backdrop of information, one who in fact time and time again is liaising with military personnel, liaising with civic authorities, we cannot compartmentalise this information into hermetically bound sections. What we have to do is in fact look at it in its entirety. Knowledge is never compartmentalised in a brain like this. It is a case of looking at the entire information that is available and coming to the conclusion that there was a sufficiency of information that would have in fact activated and triggered a need for further investigation. And what about what we may call the clear and objective indicators that detainees were being murdered? According to the Trial Chamber's findings, there were traces of blood in the KP Dom, in the vehicle that was alleged to be transporting meat. They rejected that particular position. One -- not to mention in fact the multi-faceted forms of brutality and the results like screams and cries and all that. Not to mention, for example, the real physical evidence of bullets, bullet holes behind the administration -- administration building. And all this is taken into consideration, that in fact the appellant's office is right above. The appellant's office looks into the courtyard. The appellant's office looks into the courtyard where in fact daily roll is taken. The appellant in fact is fully aware that beatings are taking place. And this is not a case where, for example, the appellant is in fact a veritable transient in this camp. He is the camp commander. And there is no evidence that in fact attempts were made to conceal these crimes. There were abundant signs of the type and nature of crimes committed, and these were clearly visible even to the eye of an uninformed and neutral observer, let alone a person in authority in the camp. Because the Trial Chamber did in fact delineate very emphatically the fact that he was a warden for some 15 months, that in fact he had unfettered access to the canteen, to the prison yard, to the compound. All those places where in fact he could have seen the signs of abuse, an abuse which in fact would put any individual on inquiry that people may in fact die as -- may die as a result or may have been killed as a result. And all this is in fact -- the unreasonableness of the Trial Chamber's findings made even clearer if the information that was provided to him is viewed together, as I said, with all those visible objective indicators of murders. If in fact we were to use the standard of Celebici, what more alarming information can there be? Had the respondent followed up that information, he would have certainly obtained further information confirming the commission of murders as I've mentioned before. Now, one may consider, for example, that the respondent's lack of knowledge with regard to the killings may have in fact been lost on the Trial Chamber because of their -- what I might call in fact tacit obsession, if I may so describe it, that in fact he kept his head in the sand. He buried his head in the sand to avoid the responsibilities of the command which accompanied the position. The Prosecution submits that it is this attitude that was reflected, for instance, in the respondent's replies to questions posed by RJ, which were described by the Trial Chamber at paragraphs 344 and 345 of the judgement; basically, don't ask. What is indicated here is that the respondent is depicted as a superior through no fault of his own, is ignorant of the events involving his subordinates, but rather and more blatantly as a superior who is confronted with abundant indications, simply does not want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be very grateful if counsel could slow down just a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Again I apologise humbly. Apart from that, Your Honours, the particular appellant had the confidence of one particular witness, RJ. Now, when you look at, for example, how RJ was looked at by the Trial Chamber, obviously they believed his evidence, and they had no doubt about -- about the veracity of his evidence. What is important, though, is that RJ was a constant -- represented a type of constant stream of information with regard to what was going on in the camp. In fact, it was RJ who indicated that Burilo was in fact one of the more brutal camp guards. And when asked about Burilo, he told -- he told the Court, he says, "It was common knowledge that Burilo was both violent before the camp and during the camp." Now, the significance of in fact that information lends itself when one considers that it was the very Burilo who was in fact responsible for beating Ekrem Zekovic, the very man in fact who everyone knows in fact was a very violent creature. And Celebici makes reference to that, that if in fact a superior is aware of individuals with in fact a particular characteristic, that in fact that alone in itself puts him on inquiry notice. But what does Krnojelac do? He does nothing. When one considers the whole Zekovic escape affair at paragraph 233, one would appreciate that in the presence of the warden, the deputy warden Savo Todovic spoke of in fact cutting rations, cutting medical attention, solitary confinement. There was lots of beatings taking place as a result of that. And the Trial Chamber, based on their assessment of that particular incident, obviously believed that in fact all these things happened. It is significant that as much as Ekrem Zekovic's offence was not part of the indictment, it is important that in fact we appreciate that they went on to conclude that although in fact they do not take the incident in relation -- into account in relation to counts 2, 4, 5, and 7, the evidence remains in this case" - this is in paragraph 230 - "as material from which inferences may legitimately be drawn by the Trial Chamber in relation to issues arising out of other incidents which are the subject of charges in this indictment." So that while correctly identifying the applicable legal standard, the Trial Chamber appears to have demanded that the respondent possess specific knowledge of the murders in order to establish his criminal liability under 7(3). It is the humble submission of the Prosecution that this approach is inconsistent with existing jurisprudence on the degree of knowledge required by a superior for liability under Article 7(3). The superior need only have information of a general nature putting him or her on notice of the risk of crimes committed. But there is no requirement Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 123 to 129. that that information must point to any specific crime. I think when one looks generally at the cumulative effect of all the information that was in the -- in the body of the appellant, one can come to but no other conclusion. And one only reasonable conclusion that there was more than sufficient information to make him realise, for example, that in fact there was a need for an inquiry. And we are saying in fact that that information was not only in fact the likely-to-know standard but also actual information. Another thing in passing which I should mention before I end on this particular ground is that at paragraph 308, the Court held this: "The accused denied that he ever saw or heard about beatings of non-Serb detainees at the KP Dom. The Trial Chamber is satisfied, however, that the accused knew that Muslim detainees were being beaten and that they were otherwise being generally mistreated in the manner described under paragraph 5.4 through 5.29 of the indictment." And when one looks at the general treatment meted out to the detainees in the indictment that the Court found to be valid, you hear of beatings with gun butts, you hear of people becoming unconscious. RJ even went on to tell them about in fact a sad case of a retarded prisoner who was walking up some stairs, who came out of line and was brutally beaten by the guards and sent to solitary confinement. That man could have died but there was no inquiry. That was sufficient notice. So it is our position on this particular ground that there was more than sufficient information available to the Trial Chamber not based on what, in fact, new information I am putting forward but based on information, factual information, that they agreed existed and that would have left to one irretrievable conclusion that more than sufficient information. Information that was actual and information that would have put him on notice, on inquiry notice also. Without more, this is my submission on this particular ground. I will now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. To a certain extent a repetition of a previous question related to torture. Admittedly, I can't understand, I can't see the consistency in the arguments of the Prosecution in toto. On the one hand, we heard the remarkable introductory submissions by Mr. Staker related to the joint criminal enterprise. In addition to this, we had some further guidance on the definition of what is the -- what about the notion of commit in 7(1) based inter alia on the definition given by Professor Roxin. So this would lead into the direction of commit -- of committing. In your own submission related to murders or killings under 5(9), you stated that it was the Prosecution's theory that it was, under 7(1), a case for aiding and abetting the murder of detainees in the KP Dom. Now we listen that you're -- in your opinion, it's a 7(3) case, to prevent and punish. Isn't there an inconsistency in the line of arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Again, there is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: If I could take that question, Your Honour. It's a simple case that in relation to various other crimes there were charges under both Article 7(1), and Article 7(3). In relation to the killings in this instance, there were charges under both Article 7(1) and Article 7(3), but the appeal was brought only in relation to Article 7(3). That's not to say that an appeal might not have been brought in relation to Article 7(1). Our submission would be that the Prosecution by not appealing something does not mean that it might not have been appealed. It was the two convictions on the basis of aiding and abetting that raised, very directly, the question of what is the difference between aiding and abetting and participation in a joint criminal enterprise. And it was because those convictions so directly raised that question that they formed the subject of that ground of appeal. I would submit that by not appealing Article 7(1) in relation to other crimes, that is not inconsistent with the Prosecution's theory, because the Prosecution is not saying that they could not have been Article 7(1). It's simply the case that the Prosecution hasn't included those in its appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the indulgence given to me with regard to time, I will try to be -- sorry. I will try to be as short as I can on the eighth ground of appeal which is in fact the ground of sentence. I should begin and indicate, for example, that to a large extent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As quickly as you can, but you must finish by 1.00. There is no choice. There is no other choice. You have to finish by 1.00. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes. Much obliged. The eighth ground of appeal is one that deals with sentence. The Trial Chamber sentenced the respondent to a single sentence of imprisonment for 7.5 years. Our particular ground is that the Trial Chamber erred in imposing a sentence which did not reflect the gravity of the offences and the degree of the respondent's culpability and that it further erred in taking certain factors into account in sentencing. No one doubts, for example, that the Trial Chamber has in fact a wide discretionary power in the area of sentencing, but as Goran Jelisic said in paragraph 96, "A sentence should not be capricious or excessive." In fact, it is the submission of the Prosecution that an overindulgent recourse to mitigating factors or non-consideration or devaluation of aggravating circumstances may well create such a situation resulting in an obviously unduly lenient sentence. I am simply putting forward a question to the learned -- to Your Honours. Basically, as a general-type test to determine, for example, the legitimacy or in fact the reasonableness, rather, of the sentence that was given. And the question I would ask is simply this: Would right-thinking members of the public with full knowledge of the relevant facts and circumstances learning of this sentence consider that something has gone wrong with the administration of justice? Because it is our contention that the sentence imposed must reflect the inherent gravity of the criminal conduct of the accused, and determining the gravity of the crime it requires a consideration of the particular circumstances of the case as well as the form and degree of the participation of the accused in the crime. In this regard, the Prosecution has indicated that it finds certain errors with regard to how sentences -- the sentence was assessed and evaluated by the Trial Chamber. We are submitting that the first -- that there were essentially four errors. The first error is to be found in paragraphs 514 to 516 which spoke about countervailing factors that mitigated or tempered the aggravating factor of his superior responsibility. The Trial Chamber referred to his conformist personality and as much as in fact they indicated that it would not have been -- it wouldn't have in fact been treated as a mitigating factor, they said, for example, however, that it would cause them to place less weight than it otherwise would on aggravating factors. It is the submission of the Prosecution that this ultimately had the effect of leading to the imposition of a lower sentence that would have been imposed had it not have been taken into account. The Prosecution submits it is not within the proper exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion to give weight to these factors in the particular circumstances of this case. The respondent voluntarily accepted his position, fully aware of, in fact, what his responsibilities were. He was told that they were prisoners, for example. They were there because they were Muslims. The Trial Chamber rejected claims that work orders given to him could have been refused, because in fact we have evidence that there were, in fact, two previous individuals who were offered the particular position in the form of -- in the form of Veselin -- Veselin Cancar and another individual and they refused and there was no subsequent admonishment or warning or punishment for the individuals refusing the particular portfolio. In any event, if the case is that human frailties and personal weaknesses could be a factor that might be given some weight in sentencing, it is our submission that this cannot be the case when it comes to commanders who have the ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with international humanitarian law. When one looks at his position where he exercised supervisory control, he had the primary responsibility for ensuring compliance, and to take such factors into account in this case fails to acknowledge the more influential effect of encouraging or promoting crimes and an atmosphere of lawlessness within the camp created by his own ongoing failure to exercise his duties of supervision. The Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber in Celebici recognised in like form that Mucic was very similar with regard to the fact that he in fact did exercise supervisory responsibility but did not in fact act it out. The second error that the Trial Chamber's blanket rejection of the effect of crimes on others apart from the victim in evaluating a crime's gravity is unduly restrictive interpretation of the concept of both harm -- the concept of both the victim and harm. In our arguments we have in fact mapped out various international instruments. We have referred to national jurisdictions. We have also referred in fact to the ICC in terms of how there is an expanding position that victims go beyond the particular individual concerned. As a result, Your Honours, we in fact would be adopting in toto the arguments that we have in fact put in our brief. Apart from that, I would make mention that in fact there were instances, especially in Krstic at paragraph 720, in Kayishema, on the 21st of May, 1999 where, for example, mention is made of in fact the role of victim, the definition of victim, and the fact that "victim" includes more than just the individual himself or herself. Celebici also makes mention of the fact that the gravity of the crime is determined in personam and is not one of universal effect acknowledged, that the assessment of the gravity of a crime could be determined by the crime's effect on the victims.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are completely unable to follow that speed. Will you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: The Celebici trial judgement, which said that the gravity of a crime is determined in personam and is not one of universal effect, acknowledge that assessment of the gravity of a crime could be determined by the crime's effect on the victim or on persons associated with the crime and their nearest relations. Your Honours, in fact it is our position with regard to the third error in the sentencing discretion that, in determining sentence, the Trial Chamber wrongly in fact gave credit to the accused for the extent to which his counsel cooperated with it and the Prosecution in the efficient conduct of his trial. We have in fact mapped out our rationale for submitting that this is in fact erroneous and we have done so not only in our substantive brief but also in fact in terms of our reply to the appellant's response. We stand by those arguments. In relation to the fourth particular area of concern where in fact comparisons were made among the various individuals who have in fact been convicted of crimes within prison-type situations, prison camp situations, we again in fact have mapped out our arguments very in extenso and we stand by them in relation to what in fact they have said. There is but one additional point, however, I wish to make in relation to the whole area of sentencing, and that has to do with the area of killings. If in fact the Trial Chamber is of the view that there was sufficient information specifically in relation to the killings and to the murders under count 8 and 10 and that therefore in fact the Trial Chamber was in fact wrong in dismissing those charges and reinstate those charges and find him guilty accordingly. We are submitting that there is one aggravating point that would need to be considered by this learned Tribunal, and that is learning that emanates from Vasiljevic, that a discriminatory state of mind may however be regarded as an aggravating factor in relation to offences for which such a state of mind is not an element. No violation of Article 3 charged in this indictment requires such a state of mind. The Trial Chamber therefore accepts that in relation to the murder conviction pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute, the accused's discriminatory state of mind constitutes an aggravating factor. So we are submitting that by virtue of the fact that he had been charged under Article 3 where, for example, there is no need for the material element of a discriminatory intent, but in those circumstances it can constitute an additional aggravating factor. Additionally, if in fact, for example, the Trial Chamber in relation to my learned colleague's submissions on torture finds that the beatings in fact reach a point of torture, as much as in fact it would not effect the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to his -- his supervisory responsibility under 7(3), it would certainly up, up the bar in relation to the type of offences that were committed by subordinates, and those offences, by virtue of torture, would be a more grievous offence and therefore that also would be another aggravating factor. Yes. Before I come -- these essentially are my submissions. However, I notice that I do have two or three minutes remaining, and my learned lead counsel wishes to just make some conclusions based on our arguments that we have in fact put forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give -- well, I have a question I'd like to ask first. You worked on the general subject of the idea of raising the sentence. You have no other details to give to the Court. You're not giving any suggestions for a specific sentence but simply that it should be raised; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed. And the Trial Chamber in fact had -- the Prosecution at trial had recommended a particular amount, time frame. But I must admit I do come from a jurisdiction where, for example, the discretion with regard to sentencing is something that resides in the body of the Tribunal and the body of the Judges. If in fact I am asked with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges, of course, determine the sentence. I don't have to tell you that, Mr. Carmona. But there are some systems, even here, in fact, sometimes where the Prosecution asks for a minimum sentence. But having said this, I have understood where you are going. Mr. Staker, do you want to make any further comments? Who wanted to make additional statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you did pre-empt me. I do in fact have a minimum in mind. I don't know if the Court wants to -- the Prosecutor has a minimum, and the minimum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Yes. I'd like you to go to the end of your thought, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: We think that, in light of the fact that Mucic got nine years, and in relation to Aleksovski, in fact he got seven, we're thinking in terms of in fact a minimum of 12 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Staker, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I'd simply add, for the benefit of the Chamber by way of winding up, a question has arisen about the scope of our theory on joint criminal enterprise in relation to the appeal as a whole. I would clarify that we are relying on the joint criminal enterprise in relation to the unlawful imprisonment, the inhumane living conditions, the forced labour, and the deportation. It follows from the submissions I made earlier that it is the Prosecution position that the killings and the tortures were also part of this joint criminal enterprise, but it was on the basis that there were no express findings in the trial judgement that the accused knew of the killings and that the accused knew of the prohibited purpose of the tortures that the appeal in relation to those crimes was confined to Article 7(3) where the Prosecution argument relates not to knowledge but to inquiry notice, had reason to know for the purposes of Article 7(3). Other than that, I would simply conclude by stating that the Prosecution's formal submissions are contained in paragraphs 10.1 and 10.2 of the Prosecution appeal brief. We make the submission there that if sentence is to be increased, this is a matter that can be decided by the Appeals Chamber in this appeal without any need to remit to a Trial Chamber. And if I cannot assist further, those are the submissions of the Prosecution in this appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If there are no further questions, we're going to adjourn until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please Madam Registrar. We are now resuming the hearing. Can everybody hear me? Yes. Fine. Thank you. After having heard the arguments of the Prosecution, we will now turn to the Defence response. You have two hours. We will take a break after an hour and a half. Who is going to take the floor? Mr. Bakrac, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In French, perhaps it would be Bakrac, but in our language it is Bakrac. Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to adjust to your language. All right. Bakrac. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, my learned friends in the Prosecution, I will now try to answer questions concerning grounds of appeal and the argument of the Prosecution expounded both in their written brief and today in oral presentation. I shall also reply to each one of the grounds of appeal. As for the first one, the first ground of appeal of the Prosecution that the Prosecution spoke about in their written brief and during today's hearing, in this regard, the Defence thinks that the argument brought forward by the Prosecution is not of such a nature to necessitate a change of the Trial Chamber of the first instance, and we, therefore, propose to reject them as unsubstantiated. To begin with, the Prosecution, when they spoke about the joint criminal enterprise, they went into the judgement of the Trial Chamber of the first instance and the decision in the Tadic case. The Defence, with all due respect, deems that basically there is no fundamental difference between the findings of the Trial Chamber and what is in point of fact the decision of the appeal judgement in the Tadic case. Therefore, the questions arises as to whether the judgement of the Trial Chamber also recognises the three categories of joint criminal enterprise regardless of whether one calls the first category as a basic form and the third category as an extended form of the JCE. We think such categorisation, we think it should be split into two categories and the first and the second would be the basic form of the JCE and the third category an extended form of a joint criminal enterprise. We do not think that it goes beyond -- that does not deviate from the jurisprudence of this Tribunal or the decision in the appeal judgement of the Tadic case. What we believe is the most important thing when it comes to establishing the liability or participation in a joint criminal enterprise is the question of the actus reus and the mens rea, that is, what the Prosecution is duty-bound to show if it wishes to prove that any acts were committed on those grounds. As for the objective elements, that is the actus reus and the elements contained in mens rea, and it can vary depending on the category of the JCE, we also believe that the judgement of the Trial Chamber did not deviate from the standard normally applied when establishing those facts. When we look at the findings of the second -- of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case to which the Prosecution refers to, it is quite clear that the criminal liability on the basis of the participation of joint criminal enterprise also necessitates that the existence of awareness and intent were present in every individual case. We therefore deem that the finding of the Trial Chamber agrees with what was established during -- in the appeals judgement in the Tadic case. The question arises as to the interpretation of the subjective element, that is, the element which concerns the intent. And we, therefore, believe that the depositions of the Prosecution in this regard are not acceptable because the intent is interpreted much too broadly and has to do with something which we do not think represents a foundation for mens rea, that is, to show that there was indeed criminal liability based on a criminal intent. It is also to us quite clear that in this case, the Trial Chamber distinguishes three types or, rather, three categories of association for criminal purposes and that it does not deviate from the findings in the appeal judgement in the Tadic case with regard to the subjective element and that the Defence wishes to lay an emphasis on that particular aspect. So with regard to the first category of the JCE is that there is intent to commit a particular crime, but this joint intent is shared by all the co-perpetrators regardless of whether we call them co-perpetrators or accomplices. What is important is the intent to perpetrate a crime. With regard to the second category, the condition for it is not only the awareness but also an intent or, rather, the will to carry out such a joint criminal enterprise, that is, the ill-treatment. My apologies. I have just been warned to slow down. So with regard to a third category, the condition is to have the intent, the volition to participate in the criminal activity and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the second category? I'm sorry, I didn't catch that. Would you go to that again? You had moved to the second category, hadn't you? I'm not sure if I got the interpretation of that. Could you repeat that again, please, the second category?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try not to get confused. I thought that what I had said with regard to the second category had already been interpreted. With regard to the second category, the precondition is, apart from the intent, there must be also volition to that effect, that is the desire to put into action such a system of criminal intent. And in the third category, again it is the intent and wish to participate in a criminal activity or the criminal intent of a group and also to promote them and also to contribute to the JCE or at any rate the crime committed by a group. Apart from the responsibility for a crime which has not been -- which had not been agreed on the basis of a joint plan. This can happen only if one takes into account all the circumstances of the case by singling out the responsibility of one or more members of the group who could foresee the consequences of their acts. Therefore, the accused will bear the consequences of such an act. In the judgement of the Trial Chamber, it transpires quite clearly from it that the judgement does not deviate from what the Prosecution is duty-bound to establish if an accused is to be pronounced guilty on the basis of his participation in the JCE, that is, his intent to participate in such an enterprise. When we talk about the intent, it is possible that here we have to face the problem of different interpretations of the notion of intent.
