And the Defence, therefore, wishes on its part to try to shed more light to it or, rather, to explain what in the Defence's opinion the intent to commit such crimes means. This subjective component is of vital importance if one is to determine the nature and the degree of responsibility of an accused. If we speak about the intent, we believe that it is necessary to establish that there is a wish that a particular crime or crimes perpetrated within a joint criminal enterprise be accepted as one's own. When we talk about the appeals judgement in the Tadic case, the Trial Chamber referred to an example of the concentration camp of Auschwitz concentration camp where the intent was also being established, although the will of co-perpetrators to commit a particular crime and where it was indicated that although it was impossible to prove that the accused had indeed identified himself with the purposes of the Nazi regime, yet the Tribunal considered him as an abettor because he did not have a specific intent to see this crime as his own. What is the principal objection of the Defence with regard to the thesis and position of the Prosecution is that fundamental difference between the notion of intent to participate and participation in a JCE and acceptance with acts which are the outcome of such a JCE. So this is this very delicate, very subtle difference between the participation in the JCE and the aiding and abetting as a form of liability under 7(1). So in order to claim that an accused participated in the second category of a JCE, it is necessary to prove that the acts committed during such a JCE are acts which he accepts and perceives as his own. With all due respect, the Prosecution has failed to prove that and has not produced a single relevant -- single piece of evidence to that effect. And that is we think the -- so we think that their position that the Trial Chamber has erred is not acceptable. We think that there is also inconsistency with regard to the objective elements regarding the role and conditions which are indispensable if a person is to be pronounced guilty on the basis of his or her participation in the JCE. The Prosecution is also duty-bound to prove that such an activity is more important with regard to the perpetration, because the co-perpetrator is somebody who in one way or the other participates in the perpetration of an act. The contribution of an individual is also functionally related to the activities of other persons, that is, they must be complementing one another in a decisive and important manner. We also think, if we refer to the appeals judgement in the Celebici case, that something more, that simple conscious participation in a general system needs to be proved. And we believe that the Prosecution was also duty-bound to prove that. In other words, one needs to prove participation in a decisive, in a fundamental manner. From all that I have just said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Guney has a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakrac, I'm trying to follow you very carefully, and you spoke about three categories as part of the joint criminal enterprise. The first has to do with the intention of committing the crime and common design. As second, you spoke about the will to apply or to follow that intention. But I did not fully understand what the third category is. You spoke about the consequences of the crime which must be foreseeable and similar things, but I want to know exactly what the third category that you're mentioning is, that is, the category that you're putting forward before this Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is precisely the third category concerning the participation in a JCE is the category where the common awareness of the perpetration of a crime, where there is a joint decision to commit a crime, but to commit a crime which is the foreseeable and logical outcome of a system within which such a crime is committed. And that is why I considered it justifiable to distinguish between this third category, the third category as an extended form of the joint enterprise as against the first two categories which are basically the same except that their object is different. The second one went into the problems of concentration camps. That is, problems involved in a particular system. So in the third category, the principal performs a crime which goes beyond the common design but is a logical and natural outcome of the initial joint criminal enterprise. So from what we have tried to point out, we come to the conclusion that the Defence thinks that the second category is not applicable to the concrete case of this Appeals Chamber, especially not in light of the fact that, apart from the theoretical debate, the Prosecution has not offered sufficient evidence to enable us to conclude beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused shared in that intent or, rather, that he played an important part in the operation of the KP Dom and the execution of the joint criminal enterprise. And this is very important. We believe that it is important to establish, and beyond any reasonable doubt, the fact that the acts that were committed within the JCE, that the accused accepted them as their own -- as his own. Excuse me. As for alleged subgrounds of the first ground of appeal in the Prosecution's brief, it speaks about the alleged error of the Trial Chamber regarding the request for additional concert. In its brief, the Prosecution applies solely a linguistic interpretation to offer a one-sided interpretation of the decision of the Trial Chamber, saying that we've been -- the Prosecution is duty-bound to prove that for each of these cases every person, together with the principals or a principal shared the awareness required to commit a particular crime. The Defence thinks that what the Appeals Chamber established in the Tadic case, to which the Prosecution refers, clearly says that a participant in the JCE in any of the three mentioned categories must share the awareness as the -- with the chief principal or principals, and that is one of the grounds for liability for the participation in a joint criminal enterprise. When the intent to participate becomes a condition sine qua non, that is quite obvious that they might also share the awareness. However, the example quoted by the Prosecution in their brief goes in the opposite direction. That is, the Prosecution quotes the example of persons who planned a crime and direct -- when persons who are planning a crime create indirect perpetrators, legal confusion, mislead the direct perpetrators and therefore induce them to commit a crime. So we say we establish such a manner of participation, a joint criminal enterprise and the need to have a shared awareness, common awareness, then those who order the crimes would be exculpated if the direct perpetrator were unaware of the true intent of the person ordering the crime. And here we went to the other to establish a criminal liability, because it is quite clear that in this particular case we're not talking about co-perpetrators or co-perpetration, because the direct perpetrators are merely tools in the hands of those who ordered the crime, and they are merely perpetrating the act, which does not relieve of responsibility those who planned and designed the crime. So in the criminal law, one cannot accept that one starts from these things which exclude the criminal liability in order to establish the criminal liability of some other persons. And we therefore believe that the example quoted by the Prosecution is not an adequate example. The Defence, in its reply to the appeal brief of the Prosecution offered an example to show how unfounded and unacceptable was such a thesis of the Prosecution. For instance, if a child under the age of 14 were to be instructed by, say, his father to commit a crime and that child is not aware that that is a crime, then it will mean, if one accepted this kind of logic, that even the person who ordered the crime, father or any other person, would not -- would not be held liable because the two persons do not share the awareness of the crime. We do not think that such a position of the Prosecution is acceptable, and therefore, it cannot be accepted as grounds for pronouncing the sentence erroneous. So in view -- in view of all the above, we think that the first instance judgement does not contain errors insofar as it establishes that the accused cannot be responsible under 7(1) as a participant in a JCE and in relation to the second category. So as for the subground of appeal concerning the alleged error about the illegitimate imprisonment, we think it was said that the criminal intent was equalised with the motive. Of course the motive cannot be the chief element of a criminal act, but it is nonetheless very important if one is to establish the true intent of the accused, that is, a motive does not help us but it does show us the way if -- show us the way to establishing the true intent of the perpetrator. We, therefore, think that the example produced by the Prosecution concerning the fact that the Trial Chamber starts from the motive or, rather, that the motive is incorporated in the essence of the crime is not acceptable and, therefore, we think that the Prosecution's position regarding the participation in the JCE are unacceptable in this regard and should therefore be rejected. If you don't mind, I'd like to move on, that is, if there are no -- any questions, I'd like to move on to the second ground of appeal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm indebted to you for an excellent argument, but tell me this and see if you can help me. A distinction is drawn between mere knowledge of an intent to commit a crime and sharing that intent. Now, we are talking of KP Dom and of a man who was warden of KP Dom. We assume that he knew of an intent to commit a crime. I think the position taken by yourself is that he did not share the intent to commit the crime. Would you think there is some difficulty in the circumstances of KP Dom of saying that a warden knew of an intent on the part of his subordinates to commit a crime in relation to inmates of KP Dom but that he did not share their intent? Is there a difficulty there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence's position is that the Prosecution hasn't established beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused was aware of the actual intentions of the perpetrators of the crimes and that therefore, we consider that he could not have shared their intent, and he could not have accepted these crimes as his own. The Trial Chamber concentrated on the issue -- on all the counts in the indictment and also on the reliability of the knowledge that the accused had given the objective circumstances and bearing in mind his acts and omissions. So it is our position that it hasn't been established beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused was fully aware, outside the context of the conflict, what the intention of the main perpetrators was. Naturally, it is clear that under such conditions the accused was aware of the conflict. He had knowledge about the context. But outside of the context of the conflict in that territory, we don't think that it has been established beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused was aware of the exact intention of the perpetrators, and we believe that given the main form of participating in the JCE in spite of such knowledge, the Defence's position is that the accused should have shared the intent. He should have agreed with such acts and accepted them as his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me see if I recollect right your position. I understand you -- I understand you now to be taking the position that the Defence, if I may call it that, is challenging both knowledge and sharing the intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes. May I continue? Thank you, Your Honours. As far as the second ground of appeal, the Prosecution's second ground of appeal is concerned, the Defence shall also concentrate on this second ground of appeal regardless of the fact that the Prosecution quite clearly made it known that they weren't requiring that the Trial Chamber's decision be revoked or revised. We believe that the Trial Chamber was correct when it decided -- when it decided that the indictment said that the accused acted with others with regard to torture, beating, and enslavement. And this all had connotations of sharing, of acting together. This is a main crime. The indictment has identified this second category that we have mentioned, and in its -- but it didn't state that it was relying on the third category of participation in a joint criminal enterprise. It is our position that the Trial Chamber's decision was correct when they decided that it would be an injustice to the accused if the Prosecution was allowed to rely on the extended form of joint criminal enterprise, which is not mentioned in the indictment but which was announced in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. As far as the Prosecution's position is concerned, we think that the Prosecution's position was wrong when they said that they should be allowed a certain amount of flexibility when drafting the indictment, and this -- which is quite contrary to the pleadings the Prosecutor in the first brief with regard to inciting a unified and rational call in order to ensure that the proceedings before the Tribunal are coherent and foreseeable. The Prosecution itself in its brief accepted that -- accepted practice is that there is an obligation that the accused be quite clearly informed in the indictment the nature and the reasons for the charges that are directed against him. So it is quite clear that this was the Prosecution's duty. The Prosecution had the obligation of quite clearly indicating in the indictment in unambiguous terms that they rely on a third form of joint criminal enterprise which is something the Prosecution failed to do. And such a position shows that the Prosecution is obliged to inform the accused in very clear terms in the indictment as to the form of responsibility he is being charged with in the indictment. The fact that someone is charged on the basis of extended participation in a JCE implies that it is necessary that the accused should be aware of the crimes concerned outside the common plan, and it's also necessary that he know which consequences of such a plan are foreseeable so that he can prepare his defence with regard to this. Naturally, with regard to this extended form, it is necessary to deal with this decisively, and the accused should be clearly informed of the nature of the charges directed against him. The nature and the reasons for the charges directed against the accused in terminological and logical terms also entail the form of his responsibility. So the Defence thinks that this extended form of responsibility on the basis of joint criminal enterprise has to be clearly indicated in the indictment because it represents the nature, the form, the reasons for which an individual is charged with certain crimes. We would also like to point out that the indictment was returned on two occasions to be revised, and in a third decision, that is to say the decision on the basis of the third objection filed by the Defence, the Trial Chamber made it known that in addition to the fact that the indictment was not quite precise, this would have consequences with regard to the final decision rendered by the Trial Chamber. For this reason, we think that the Prosecution's position is unacceptable when they say the Defence failed to react in a timely fashion with regard to the absence of this form of charges in the indictment itself. The Defence would like to refer to logic. If such an omission on the part of the Prosecution, the omission, the failure to mention in the indictment the form of joint criminal enterprise concerned, this omission would later result in the fact that the judgement -- that in the judgement the Prosecution would be informed that the accused cannot be proclaimed guilty on the basis of that third form because it was not contained in the indictment. And therefore, for these reasons it's quite illogical and contrary to the rights of the accused to say that the Defence had the obligation to inform the Prosecution in time of such an omission. The Defence does not have the obligation to make the proceedings of the accused more difficult, and therefore we think that such arguments on the part of the Prosecution are not acceptable. We think that making it clearly known what form of joint criminal enterprise is concerned, on the basis of which form of JCE the accused is charged, this should be contained in the indictment because this shows the nature and the reasons for which accused is charged. And it is on this basis that an accused can prepare his defence, on the basis of such information. And that concludes my response to the second ground of appeal. As far as the third ground of appeal is concerned, the Prosecution's third ground of appeal, the error of the Trial Chamber with regard to the crime of maltreatment, the Defence would like to say that in its brief, it emphasised the fact that the accused did not have the position of a superior with regard to the guards and non-Serbian detainees in the KPD and therefore was not authorised to issue orders to them or to control their acts or to punish their acts. But even if the findings of the Trial Chamber according to which the accused had such effective control over non-Serbian detainees and over the Serbs in the KPD who have been referred to as some of the perpetrators for crimes that were committed, even in such a case, on the basis of the facts established by the Trial Chamber, it is not possible to reach a conclusion beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused is responsible as a superior according to Article 7(3) of the Statute for counts 2 and 4, which is what is stated in the Prosecution's appeal brief. And for this reason, we think that the Prosecution's position, this position on the part of the Prosecution is erroneous and the findings of the Trial Chamber with that regard, as far as this matter is concerned, is absolutely correct. And the Defence has also pointed out to the -- a lack of legal force of the arguments presented by the Trial Chamber with regard to the established facts as far as the knowledge of the accused is concerned according to which the accused was aware of the beatings in the KPD. And in the Prosecution's brief, they have pointed out -- they have pointed three examples of beatings which were established by the Trial Chamber, and according to the Prosecution, they should represent -- this should be sufficient evidence to prove that the accused could have known that criminal acts of maltreatment were being committed in the KPD. These are three examples that the Trial Chamber has referred to as -- referred to as having been established. And the Prosecution, in its brief, also referred to these examples when it pleaded, when it argued that the -- that it had been proven beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused was responsible and, therefore, that he could have been aware of the fact that there was maltreatment in the KPD. As far as the first example is concerned with regard to these allegations that the consequences for the physical state of the -- the physical condition of the detainees could have been the result of such acts, the Defence's position is that the Prosecution with regard to such findings on the part of the Trial Chamber, it can't rely on such findings. The Prosecution can't rely on such findings, and it has been established beyond any doubt in all the other evidence presented that Muslim detainees who were taken to the KPD throughout -- almost throughout the entire period during which the accused had the position that he had, they appeared there and it was obvious that they already had traces of beatings. There were visible physical traces of the conflict, of the beatings that they had sustained. So the fact that these -- that this was visible, that it was -- that the traces were visible on these people, this fact is relevant and it indicates that the accused may have had knowledge that these beatings were taking place elsewhere. And in its appeal, we have said that it is for this reason that the accused could not be charged on the basis of beatings either, and especially given that -- and to an even lesser extent can such a finding of the Trial Chamber can be the basis for the Prosecution to claim that the accused could have and should have been aware of the crime of beatings. So there is evidence that detainees were taken to the KPD, and they already had very evident physical injuries. This evidence in itself does not present proof of any significant kind in the sense that -- or not according to the jurisprudence or the request of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. And it especially cannot prove the crime of beating, of maltreatment. The second example concerns the witness RJ referred to by the Prosecution in its oral address to the Chamber today. In the case of this witness, it was established that he informed the accused that non-Serb detainees were beaten and maltreated and that they were aware of this fact because they heard the sounds of beatings from the administrative building. And although -- if the Trial Chamber takes this into consideration, accepts this evidence, the testimony of the witness RJ, which is restrictive in our opinion, this same witness also testified that the accused told him that he was not competent for these matters but that he had borne a responsibility for these matters but that he would look into it. And the Defence considers that what the witness said to the accused was not necessarily true. And the accused did not have the obligation of accepting this without any doubt, without having any reservations about this information. Regardless of the fact that the Defence considers that the accused was not under any obligation to investigate such allegations, we think that when the Prosecution cites this example, they have not proved beyond any reasonable doubt that this piece of information is of great relevance and that an investigation should have been lunched into the allegations given the information provided. As far as the third example is concerned, that of Ekrem Zekovic, we think that this finding of the Trial Chamber is not appropriate to be taken as a basis upon which one could establish that it is a fact that the accused had knowledge of beatings being perpetrated in the KPD, especially not that he had knowledge of beatings for a forbidden objective. The Defence would like to mention that the incident that the Trial Chamber established with regard to the beating of Ekrem Zekovic, an incident which was established to have happened on the 8th or 9th of July, 1993, and the Defence has proven this with material evidence, at the time the accused was no longer even formally a warden of the KPD since the Ministry -- since on the 1st of July, 1993, he no longer had this function and he spent only a little more time in the KPD subsequent to this date. But this will be a matter of discussion, a matter of issues that the Defence will deal with in its appeal. But what we consider is essential and what must be emphasised at the moment is that such knowledge, such information, which was provided a few days before the accused left the KPD, cannot be used to retro -- cannot be used to oblige the accused to retroactively carry out investigations. He cannot be retroactively obliged to look into certain acts that may have been perpetrated. So this isolated piece of information is a piece of information he was provided with at the end of his term in the KPD and did not necessarily entail his responsibility for carrying out investigations into something that took -- that had already happened, that had happened at an earlier date. So we don't think that such an argument on the part of the Prosecution is an acceptable one. This isolated piece of information, in our opinion, cannot be accepted on a retroactive basis, and the accused cannot be charged with not having looked into the incidents given that he knew on the 8th or 9th of July, Zekovic may have been beaten for a prohibited objective and that he was therefore obliged to do something and that represented the basis on which he was responsible for all the prior excesses in the KPD. This piece of information cannot be considered to be relevant, cannot be an indication of the fact that he's responsible for all the acts that occurred in the KPD prior to that date. Thus we consider that this incident cannot a priori -- could not a priori have proven to the accused that beatings were concerned for an objective -- for a prohibitive purpose. This is Ekrem Zekovic from the KPD who is concerned, who the guard Burilo beat up when he arrived in the KPD according to the findings of the Trial Chamber. And the accused appeared at the moment that that was happening, at the time that this act was being perpetrated. So the Prosecution has not established beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused, even if he had carried out such an investigation would necessarily have obtained information that what was at stake were beatings in order to attain a prohibited objective. What the Defence wants to point out here is that the Prosecution, in legal terms, has given a far too broad interpretation of legal standards as far as establishing responsibility of the accused is concerned. We believe that given the fact and given the facts that perhaps the accused was aware that there were beatings, we don't think that on this basis the Prosecution can conclude that the accused, had he conducted an investigation, would necessarily have had to find out that certain beatings were carried out for a prohibited objective. These assumptions that the Trial Chamber did not want to consider and thus we don't think that they made an error and it is for this reason that we suggest that this ground of appeal on the part of the Prosecution also be rejected. I would now like to move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Guney would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakrac, under 3 and 4 here you said that the accused did not have power over the guards and that he had no power in order to prevent the criminal acts which were being committed. And so that power, that is, his prerogatives were very limited. Could you compare the powers and prerogatives of the accused as the warden of the KP Dom? Can they be seen positively? According to you as the Defence, what were the powers and prerogatives of the accused as the warden of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you list them quickly, what his powers were, the powers that he had as the warden?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I will attempt to answer this question, although the Defence has dealt with this issue exhaustively in its first ground of appeal in its appeal brief. There are witness statements, statements given by Defence witnesses, and there's material evidence that indicates that part of the KPD had been leased to the army and to the military authorities in order to detain Muslims there, or rather, non-Serbian civilians, and there is a lot of material evidence which the Defence has attempted to present to show the Trial Chamber that the accused had no control over that part of the KPD. Perhaps there was a misunderstanding in that the Defence is not pleading and is not claiming that there was some clear-cut physical division that occurred, that this fact is reflected in particularly with regard to the rights and the authority of the accused within the framework of that institution. The Defence has provided the Trial Chamber with a number of proofs that show that the military authorities were in charge of exchanges. They also compiled lists of persons and established who would be released and when. Permission to visit was also issued by the military authorities, and the Defence has proven this by using a lot of evidence. So there is not a single piece of evidence presented by the Prosecution that would show that the accused played a role of any kind in organising the part of the KPD where Muslim detainees were being held or that he had authority of any kind there. And with the permission of the Appeals Chamber, the Defence will also indicate how numerous this, how voluminous this evidence is. And with all the other evidence we have, it shows that the accused had no authority, was not competent for that part of the KPD, and he had absolutely no authority whatsoever with regard to the detained Muslims and with regard to the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just a very short follow-up question. I think we should always bear in mind that we are acting as an Appeals Chamber here and therefore, in principle, are bound by the facts found by the Trial Chamber, and the threshold to reverse the factual findings is extremely high, and I want to draw your attention to your conclusion which is a conclusion of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 107 that the accused exercised supervisory responsibility over all subordinate personnel and detainees in the KP Dom. However, coming back to the question of -- asked by my colleague Judge Guney. In paragraph 98, the question is whether or not the Trial Chamber came to this conclusion in the proper way. And there we can read that there was an appointment by the Ministry of Defence, and the Trial Chamber did not achieve -- have the necessary documents that they would need. And I quote paragraph 98: "The Defence said that it would seek to obtain these documents upon which the Ministry of Defence relied to offer the certificate for tender at that stage. These documents were never produced and the Defence does not seek to enter the certificate into evidence at any later stage. The Trial Chamber takes these circumstances into account when coming to the conclusion." My question is: Isn't it the opinion of the Defence that this way of arguing in this very limited sphere would lead to place the burden of proof to the Defence rather than the Prosecution? And my question is: Did you identify in the factual findings any findings in support of your legal submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I find it a little embarrassing to repeat it, and I think that the Defence, when it comes to presenting its brief, will point at a large bulk -- large evidence and very many other things which bring me to question the decision of the Trial Chamber. The onus was on the Prosecution, and they had to prove not only de jure responsibility but also the de facto responsibility of the accused. I touched up on the third ground of appeal of the Prosecution as to the form of indictment, and the Trial Chamber has warned the Prosecution that they could not and should not rely merely on his title of a prison warden, that they were bound to prove his true authority over certain individuals. The Defence on its part has undertaken to prove the innocence of the accused or, rather, the onus to prove that apart from his de jure role, his de facto role did not exist and that here we were dealing with two completely different systems of chain of command, because the defence has produced evidence to show that the accused was appointed to the position of a warden by the Minister of Justice. And the part of the KP Dom where non-Serb prisoners were kept was leased to the army and the army exercised authority over those individuals. Furthermore, the Defence, through the testimony of guards, and they testified here before the Chamber, and we also produced some evidence to show that even the security guards in the KP Dom were appointed by the military authority. And that is why we claimed, alongside other evidence, that the accused had no authority over these guards nor that he had any resources, any means at his disposal to punish them for whatever transgression that they had committed and he had learnt about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I only wanted to alert you that it would be in favour of your client not to try to replace the findings by the Trial Chamber by your own factual submissions during appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. So insofar as the fourth ground of appeal is concerned, killings; the Defence deems, as in the previous cases, in this ground the Prosecution refers to allegations and indicia endeavouring to use some facts, some information that the accused might possibly have raised to the level of alarming information and which would then lay down the standard for mens rea, that is are allowed to bring charges against the accused under 7(3) of the Statute. So all that was mentioned here with regard to the previous two grounds of appeal with regard to the shifting the onus of proving some facts, an unduly broad approach, we think the same argument is applicable also in this case, and the Defence thinks all of this can be said also of the fourth ground. In its fourth ground, the Prosecution analysed the Trial Chamber's finding as to the position of the accused as a person who had certain powers in the KP Dom and said that part of the KP Dom, the fact that part of it was leased to the army affected little the hierarchy in the KP Dom. The Prosecution says it had little effect, but we practically think that the fact that part of the KP Dom was leased must have had some effect on the powers. This fact, however, needs to find its reflection in the status, establishing whether the information available to the accused was of such nature that it could be applied under the mens rea standard to be able to charge the accused under 7(3). This fact had to find its reflection also in the nature of information. It has to do both with this ground of appeal of the Prosecution and -- so the duty to inform. And a sufficient number of alarming and adequate information that we referred to in replying to the third and fourth grounds of appeal also holds true in relation to the fifth ground of appeal of the Prosecution. In this case, the Prosecution relied on the findings of the Trial Chamber which said that for 15 months the accused was the warden of the penitentiary, of the KP Dom, and that the widespread excesses both in time and space could really provide you with sufficient information that such acts might have indeed been committed in the KP Dom. The Trial Chamber also established that 26 killings happened during a relatively short period of time, that is end of July and beginning of August 1992. The Defence does in no way wish to underestimate the severity of this crime and the effects, but the Defence knows that we are talking about 26 killings which happened over two, three, or maybe four evenings in -- towards the end of June and early July 1992. These facts does not show that the killings were so widespread both in time and space that one should take it that the accused had enough possibility, enough opportunity to come by sufficient information in this regard, especially when one bears in mind that these killings were performed during a few evenings at a specified period of time when the accused was not present in the KP Dom as has been established. So in itself, it cannot lead us to a valid conclusion that the accused had at his disposal sufficient information that would, if nothing else, warn him that some of his subordinates were committing murders. Furthermore, the additional element which is the one that the Prosecution indicates as possible indicia that such killings were happening during the relevant period of time of KP Dom once again do not lead us to a conclusion that the accused had sufficient and alarming information that such crimes were taking place. The Prosecution also invokes additional elements such as marks and traces in KP Dom or evidence in KP Dom a car with an exhaust pipe which was broken, and with some bloodstains, then screams and cries of pain, bullet traces in the walls of corridors and the metal door in the administrative building, and so on. All of these are elements which could not tell the accused, which did not constitute sufficient and alarming information that murders were being committed in the KP Dom. The Prosecution has failed to show that the accused, although he had access to the canteen and the yard of the KP Dom, was necessarily informed and aware of these traces and marks. That is, this could not be something that will be the subject of his direct observation. Bullet markings on the walls of the KP Dom need not have meant alarming and sufficient information that murders were being committed in the KP Dom. The shots that were heard at night when he was there once again do not suffice to show that -- did not suffice to be termed as alarming and sufficient information telling the accused that crimes were being committed in the KP Dom. In other words, we think that all these things that the Prosecution relies on cannot be interpreted as information that was adequate and necessary to start an investigation for crimes, and they have also failed to show that the accused was aware of all these details to do anything. All that is said in the Prosecution's brief in this regard could not constitute information at all, because such information never reached the accused. That is, the Trial Chamber has not found that this information reached the accused. It has not found it beyond any reasonable doubt. And in particular, we do not think that these -- that this is worrying, alarming information that would be indicative of killings committed by persons subordinate to the accused Krnojelac. In their brief and today, the Prosecution mentioned that the accused was -- knew of a death which occurred under suspicious circumstances and pointed out that the accused had learnt from a nurse that the person had committed suicide. We think that the Prosecution has once again failed to show that such information which the accused obtained from a nurse could be -- could constitute an alarming piece of information which would then bind him to conduct investigation in order to establish whether killings indeed were happening in the KP Dom. If we went along with such an interpretation of the Prosecution that some signs such as revolver shots at night or bullet marks on the walls of the KP Dom, which is as was established by the Trial Chamber, which was shelled during the armed conflict, we still cannot agree that they're representing round to claim that the accused is responsible under 7(1), that he can be held responsible for these killings, and we therefore think that this ground of appeal of the Prosecution should also be rejected as lacking foundation. Now I'd like to move on to the next ground of appeal of the Prosecution, that is if there are no questions by the members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, should I understand you this way, that your position is the question whether there was alarming information was one of fact to be evaluated by the Trial Chamber and that the Appeals Chamber cannot intervene unless it is satisfied that no reasonable Tribunal of fact could have found otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to follow up on Judge Shahabuddeen's question. To be clear, there are errors of fact which you do tend to bring out in response to what the Prosecutor said, but I recall what I said to you at the beginning of our hearing this morning, as Judge Schomburg has already told you and as Judge Shahabuddeen has told you; in terms of errors of fact, keep in mind that would be related to a trier of fact. For example, if there was a suicide in a prison in an administrative system which would be reasonably constituted, would that cause the higher authorities to be alerted to what had happened? That would be a criteria which could be of interest to a Chamber. When there is a suicide in a prison, perhaps one could imagine that an administrative system in a democratic well organised country there would be an alarm system. Those are the types of criteria that you should bring us back to but not to again plead what was already pleaded so well by yourself. And I said this also to the Prosecutor. Having said this, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Should I move on to the next ground of appeal or -- thank you, Your Honour. The fifth ground of appeal of the Prosecution deals with persecution and beatings. The Defence deems that the Prosecution has no evidence, that is, has produced no objective and solid facts and, therefore, it wishes to shift the burden of proof to the Defence in this ground, and they rely merely on some assumptions deriving from some general circumstances and general facts which have been found. Ergo, we think that what the Prosecution claims under this ground runs counter to legal principles and international customary law, that is, principles which can also find in modern legislations but which existed also in the Roman law, that is in dubio pro reo; if I doubt then it must be in favour of the accused. What is the basis of the Prosecution's fifth ground of appeal moves in the opposite direction. If in doubt, then -- then it will incriminate the accused further. That is what we believe, and we believe it because the Prosecution does not corroborate their views with concrete facts and circumstances which would persuade the Trial Chamber to change the decision of the first instance Chamber. That is, in their fifth ground the Prosecution objects to the finding of the Trial Chamber and says that the interpretation of the Trial Chamber was too narrow and that things were not viewed within a broader context within which some fundamental acts took place. And therefore even if it comes from the Prosecution but the Defence finds surprising the objection that in this case the Trial Chamber, as the Prosecution says, applied a narrow and legalistic, discriminatory, that is, approach. We think that the Trial Chamber could not apply any other approach but the one which the Prosecution objects to in this ground of appeal. In the Defence's view, the Prosecution said that discrimination based on racial or ethnic basis should be interpreted in the broadest possible way on the basis of assumptions so as to alleviate the Prosecution's burden of proof so that they would need to invest less effort in proving that this crime happened. The Trial Chamber established in judgement that there was a persecution as a crime against humanity as shown in imprisonment and inhumane living conditions. When the Trial Chamber established that the detention of non-Serbs in the KP Dom was the result of discrimination and the inhumane acts relative to living conditions also were the result of discriminatory policies. If we bear in mind this finding of the Trial Chamber which has to do with the discrimination underpinning the crime of detention and inhumane living conditions, then it is quite unacceptable to use it to draw the conclusion that all the other acts envisaged by the statute of this Tribunal were committed as forms of discrimination without having to establish concrete facts, and only on the basis of the discrimination-driven imprisonment and the inhumane living condition. The fact that the Trial Chamber has already established that the accused was responsible for persecution as a crime against humanity in view of the imprisonment and inhumane living conditions; no. It must necessarily -- it makes it indispensable to establish that all the other acts, all the other things that were done in KP Dom were also driven by desire for discrimination. Now, we think that it is the duty of the Prosecution to establish clearly that each one of these acts which are -- with which the accused is charged were based on discrimination and driven by discrimination. The Defence tried to respond to this. It is quite possible that the living conditions in the KP Dom, in detention in a small milieu, we're talking about the town of Foca and its surroundings, it is quite possible that being a Serb guard and a detained Muslim might have come to settling perhaps some old scores, those which existed even before the conflict. So one need not necessarily assume, since the detainees are non-Serbs, Muslims guarded by Serbs, any act which could be interpreted as a crime under the statute of this Tribunal could not have been based on discrimination. It is the duty of the Prosecution, the Defence deems, to, in every concrete case, for every count of the indictment, for everything that it charges the accused with, to prove that that act was based on discrimination, was done with a view to discrimination and was driven by discrimination. It is unacceptable that the Prosecution claims -- when the Prosecution from indisputable facts, that there were two groups that were opposed to each other in a conflict, to then draw general conclusion and they cannot draw the conclusion that because certain acts were committed they must have been -- they could not have been committed except for reasons of discrimination. So these assumptions, the Prosecution may not raise these assumptions to a higher level, to a level of found facts. They must provide proof to show that these acts were the fruit of discrimination, that these acts were committed with a view to discrimination and for no other reason or motive. So it is clear why the Prosecution says that it is not necessary to prove that every individual act was based on discrimination, because the fact that all these acts were very widespread is showing this discrimination itself. We do not think that such a broad system of evidence, of proof can be accepted and we do not think that the burden of proving is now shifted to the Defence. We do not think that it is acceptable. It is not up to the Defence to have to prove that every act that is laid at the door of the accused was committed -- was not committed for a discriminatory reason. It is up to the Prosecution to offer proof that a particular act was committed with such intentions in mind. So this would be our answer to the fifth Prosecution's ground of appeal, and perhaps it is now time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We think that it is time for the break which will resume at half past four, and then you will have another half hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in. I was a bit too generous with you, Mr. Prosecutor, when I gave you more time, but I'm sure that with the ability you have to summarise things -- I mean Defence, that is -- you will be able to finish in the limited time scheduled today. Tomorrow you will have as much time as the Prosecutor had this morning. All right. So we can hear you until about 5.00, and then there will be the final reply of the Prosecution. All right. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Given what you have said, I will say in advance for each ground of appeal that I stand by the allegations -- the statements that I made in my written response to the Prosecution's appeal. I'll try and summarise the essence of what the Defence wanted to present before you. The next ground of appeal concerns persecution based on forced labour. The main objection in the Defence's view made by the Prosecution has to do with the voluntary nature of performing the work, and the Trial Chamber established that such work was in fact carried out in the KPD. Supporting its claims with regard to the absence of the voluntary nature of such work, we think that the Prosecution, when it charged the accused with this crime, compared it to the crime of rape, and this was inappropriate, the crime of rape which is the subject of jurisprudence in this Tribunal and with regards to which an appeals judgement was reached in the Kunarac case. If a parallel is established without any restrictions between those two crimes, we think it is not appropriate, and we do not believe that the Prosecution can base itself on such a situation. But we do consider that unlawful confinement and inhumane conditions by themselves do not make -- do not deprive the Prosecution of the obligation to establish a certain degree of voluntary work. The degree of criminal responsibility isn't adequate and can't be irrelevant for establishing whether the crime of forcing people to work was committed. The Prosecution attempted to use many examples of errors committed by the Trial Chamber with regard to facts which the Trial Chamber established through a number of witnesses. They negate -- and to negate that this work was voluntary, in our opinion, was done in a way that doesn't show that the accused could be proclaimed guilty on the basis of these crimes. On the contrary, on the basis of all the examples provided by the Prosecution and in the findings of the Trial Chamber, one can see that none of these witnesses refused to work. On the contrary, we have information according to which all of them, for various personal reasons, wanted to work. The very fact that the civilians in the KPD were detained without there being a legal basis for this, and the fact that the living conditions were -- were very poor cannot -- does not mean that the Prosecution doesn't have the obligation to prove that people were forced to work and that such -- and that the reason for forcing them to work was of a discriminatory nature. I apologise. I have been warned to slow down again. And I would also like to apologise to the interpreters. I'm trying to say as much as I can in a short period of time. It was for the Prosecution to prove that this work was forced. If the Prosecution enumerates various motives, which is what it does in its brief, it cannot claim that the circumstances were such that no one worked on a voluntary basis. From the examples of the Trial Chamber, from the findings of the Trial Chamber, one can see that all the individuals for whom the Trial Chamber decided they worked, it can be seen that they had a motive to work. Some of them worked in order to obtain better food, others in order to be able to circulate more freely. There were others who wanted to work in order to find out more information. So there is not a single reason, for example fear of being punished. One can't say that they all worked because they were afraid of being punished. There were a number of reasons, a number of subjective reasons. These people worked for a variety of reasons and motives. So the living conditions in the KPD, the fact that they were unlawfully detained, by themselves do not indicate, do not prove that the work was forced. On the contrary, in our opinion, the Prosecution does not have a single piece of evidence to support the claim that the work was forced. The Trial Chamber's findings were correct when they said that the individuals worked on a voluntary basis and that this was confirmed by the individuals involved in the work. The reasons for which they worked cannot play a decisive role in deciding on the criminal responsibility of the accused. The basis of this complaint is the idea of persecution based on compulsory work. The Prosecution should have proved that this forced labour was of a discriminatory nature, that its purpose was discrimination. The Defence could just like to point out very briefly, and I do not want to diminish the gravity of the crimes established by the Trial Chamber, the gravity of the crimes that occurred in the KPD, but I would like to emphasise that the fact that the Trial Chamber established that there were over 500 -- or between 500 and 700 Muslims in the KPD and that about -- well, perhaps between -- about 50 individuals were involved in the work - that's about 10 per cent - this proves the contrary. This proves that the reason for which the detained civilians were discriminated against, if the reason for making them work was of a discriminatory nature, then each one of them would have had to perform tasks of a certain kind, carry out work. In our brief, the Defence, with regard to the functioning of the Drina Economic Unit, mentioned -- we mentioned that economic unit, and it is possible to decide what the background of this work was, the background of the work in which a number of people were involved. So we don't think that the Prosecution can support its claims with established facts. And it is also our opinion that this can't be a basis for the Trial Chamber's decision to be reversed. And thus we suggest, given all the arguments presented by the Defence in its written response, we suggest that this be rejected as a basis for reversing the decision. I would like to move on to the following ground of appeal, the following ground of appeal of the Prosecution to which the Defence responds is the crime of deportation as persecution. I believe that the Prosecution when discussing this ground of appeal concentrated on certain terms, on certain ideas of deportation. I think that the Appeals Chamber assisted to quite an extent when clarifying the position of the Prosecution with regard to this matter. In the opinion of the Defence, the Defence in its response to the Prosecution brief also developed a -- expanded on a number of these issues, and we also believe that this ground cannot be accepted, and we believe that the Prosecution has not demonstrated that the decision of the Trial Chamber with regard to this ground was incorrect and should be reversed or revised. The Prosecution's position with regard to the crime of deportation is that the issue of international borders, the issue of the location, it concerned the issue of the location to which certain individuals were sent. They claimed that this -- it wasn't important whether this location was beyond the state borders or not in order to establish the existence of such a crime. I think that such an approach would result in many problems with regard to establishing the responsibility of the accused. In a specific example, in a given example if we accepted the Prosecution's position, according to which deportation is just the forcible transfer of a given individual regardless of the location or regardless of the location or regardless of the destination to which this individual is transferred, then we can reach the conclusion that deporting, transferring Muslims from their flats to the KPD already amounts to a form of deportation. So for that group for which the -- with regard to that group for which the accused is not responsible, we have already established that there was the crime of deportation. They are transferred from their flats to an institution where they were unlawfully detained, and given the Prosecution's position, this amounts to deportation. The fact that these people were released from the KPD, from prison, from living in such conditions amounts to deportation. This is contrary to the indisputable fact that these individuals were taken from their flats, from their homes to an institution where they were unlawfully detained in inhumane conditions. Releasing them from such an institution is not something that can -- for which an accused can be considered to be criminally responsible, given exchanges that occurred, because the alternative was to detain them in such inhumane conditions, in conditions of unlawful detention. So preventing these people to be transferred would result in the criminal responsibility for another act. And the Prosecution has pleaded about, has argued with regard to this matter, and the accused has been declared responsible for this act. If one viewed deportation in the way that the Prosecution views deportation, then there would be kind of equivalence between deportation and unlawful detention, because those people were taken, were transferred from their flats to the KPD and they were unlawfully detained there. And that is why I believe that this ground of appeal presented by the Prosecution, and it refers to the crime of persecution and deportation, this ground of appeal should also be rejected and be considered to be unfounded. If there are no further questions, I would move on to the last ground of appeal presented by the Prosecution, which refers to the decision on the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Bakrac. I was interested in your proposition that if the Prosecution were right, then there would be an act of deportation as soon as an inmate was transferred to the KP Dom. Is there a difficulty in this sense, that the act of deportation might be thought to mean the forcible removal of a person from one living environment to another living environment in which he will have to live? He wouldn't be having to live in KP Dom, would he?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. However, the essence of what the Defence wanted to say in its response to the Prosecution is that, first of all, the transfer, the Defence expanded on this in greater detail in its written response to the Prosecution's brief. We explained that transfer can also be permitted if it is done for security reasons or if it is done because it is necessary for military reasons, and thus the Prosecution with regard to this matter was also obliged to establish, to demonstrate that these transfers from the KPD, the exchanges, in fact, weren't transfers of a permanent kind in the sense required by the crime of deportation. It didn't meet the standards required by the crime of deportation. On the contrary, these exchanges which involve taking people from the KPD to the territory which is not under the control of the people in the KPD, in itself this is not a sufficient reason to apply the standard of deportation in accordance with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As far as the last ground of appeal of the Prosecution is concerned, in which they mention the fact that the Trial Chamber violated its right of discretion on four occasions, and the Prosecution in its response to the brief provided an interpretation according to which, given that the accused was a warden in the generic sense of the term and as a superior he was responsible for all the subordinates and the detainees in the KPD, for this reason it was not possible to say that there were mitigating circumstances. We think that the Trial Chamber didn't commit this first error and that such response on the part of the Prosecution has no foundation. Given that the position of the accused, in fact, the position of the accused as a warden is already contained in the essence of the crime, that is to say the accused as a superior was proclaimed, was declared guilty. Thus his responsibility in that sense was established. And it is contained in the essence, in the substance of the crime, that is to say in the basis of his responsibility according to 7(3), Article 7(3). So there is no reason for the Trial Chamber to be allowed -- to allow reasons of a personal nature to determine the decision on the sentence. It is for these reasons that the Defence does not believe that the Trial Chamber considered an error with regard to this issue. As far as the argument that the Trial Chamber in its judgement committed another error with regard to the application of its discretion to measure the crime, the judgement, and that it didn't have any relevance for the criminal consequences, we also believe that the idea of a victim in terms of international law, international criminal law, is already incorporated in the acts, in what the acts represent. So the responsibility for some of the violations of international law that are treated as war crimes, this is already incorporated, everything that such a crime represents. These include the sufferings of the victims and of the families. So in addition to the fact that this has already been incorporated into the nature of the crime for which the accused has been declared responsible, this cannot be considered as an aggravating factor. As far the third area is concerned, as far as the application of discretionary right is concerned, which according to the Prosecution refers to participation and the efficient act in the Defence of the accused and objection that this position of the Trial Chamber has exceeded its discretionary right, we also think that it hasn't been supported by arguments. It is clear that the Defence must behave in accordance with the code of their profession in front of the Trial Chamber, and this includes cooperation. This includes cooperating and acting efficiently before the Trial Chamber and participating with the various parties, but it is also clear, I think, it's the Defence's position that the Trial Chamber had this in mind, that the Defence should legally articulate the attempts and the strivings of its client, of the accused. The accused is the person who could have requested from the Defence that certain matters be investigated, that indisputable events be investigated and thus the work of the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber, would have been rendered more difficult. So such cooperation is the result of a request on the part of the accused, a request according to which anything that he thought was established beyond a doubt, doubt shouldn't be cast on this. I think that this is what the Trial Chamber had in mind and that is something which in the legislative system from which I come is considered to be a mitigating factor. It concerns the behaviour of the accused before the Trial Chamber, his assistance to the Trial Chamber, and it concerns whether or not he has facilitated the proceedings, facilitated the conclusion of the proceedings. I think that the Trial Chamber, given that they took as a mitigating factor, I think that they -- by doing that, they did not violate their discretionary right when determining the sentence. In the Defence's position, the Prosecution's thesis that the Trial Chamber committed a fourth error is not acceptable with regard to its discretionary right to apply a sentence, because the Trial Chamber did not show the gravity of the crimes committed by the accused in its judgement. We think that the gravity of the crimes and the degree of criminal responsibility of the accused, the degree to which he participated in the crimes, we consider -- we believe that this determined the decision in this case, and that is something that is the right of the Trial Chamber. In this specific case and on the basis of the established facts, it has the right to establish the degree of responsibility of the accused and the gravity of the acts perpetrated. Or to be simple, a certain degree of participation within a group of crimes provided for in the Statute of this Tribunal. The Prosecution believes that the sentence -- the seven-year sentence meted out to Zlatko Aleksovski influenced the decision and they mentioned that that sentence would have been high if he hadn't been charged on two occasions, cumulatively twice. If the Prosecution claims that in each specific case the Trial Chamber should have the discretionary right to measure, to decide on the appropriate sentence, on the sentence that is appropriate for the circumstances of a given case, then this case could be described as similar to the other case in general terms. But both cases have their special circumstances and factors which are relevant for whether the sentence should be large or not so large. If there are these mitigating factors which influenced the Aleksovski judgement, then there are mitigating factors in this case which cannot be taken into account in the Aleksovski case. The Defence will mention the direct participation. It was stated that in the Aleksovski judgement that Aleksovski was personally present at the scene of certain crimes, crimes which must also be valued and compared. And the Trial Chamber didn't establish that Krnojelac was physically present or participated directly in any of the acts that he is charged with. The Prosecution also denied that it was possible for the Trial Chamber to draw a parallel between the sentence in the Kvocka case, because that sentence is not final yet. However, the Prosecution may not disregard the fact that in that case in which the accused Kvocka was sentenced to seven years, that there has been no appeal whatsoever, not even appeal against sentence. From the point of view of the Prosecution, as said, we can say that for the Prosecution, that case has been concluded. Therefore, we do not think that their claim that the Trial Chamber erred when comparing cases which seem to be the same, if one looks at all the facts which are common to all of them and those which are specific to all of them, that they determine the sentence. We do not think that the Chamber erred in this regard, and I believe that this ground should be rejected, all the more so as we heard today something that was not addressed in the written brief of the Prosecution, that is, a suggestion as regards the sentence, 12 years. And I do not think this had been properly argued, and therefore I think that suggestion should also be rejected. But after all, it is the Appeals Chamber which will decide on the sentence regardless. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. And now I turn to the colleagues. I want to turn to the Prosecution and ask if you wish to exercise your right to respond. You do not have to if you do not wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you very much, Your Honour. The Prosecution does intend briefly to exercise its right to reply, and with the Appeals Chamber's permission, we propose to address each of the grounds of the appeal in the same order and with the same speakers as our principal submissions. I'll then proceed to with grounds 1 and 2. With relation to ground 1, my understanding is that my colleague counsel for the defence does accept the existence in law of the three categories of joint criminal enterprise liability identified in the Tadic appeal judgement, and that the issue in this case is one of the interpretation of the elements and their application to the facts. I understand that the Defence takes issue with one element of the actus reus. It was said by my colleague for the Defence that participation in a joint criminal enterprise must be such that the participants are complementing each other in an important manner and that the contribution must be decisive or fundamental. In answer to that, I'd refer to the fact that in my principal submissions I did cite paragraphs 127 and 171 of the trial judgement in which the Trial Chamber made the finding of fact that there was a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, and indeed, in paragraph 171, that it was substantial. I don't want to repeat my principal submissions, but I did refer to the paragraphs of the trial judgement stating the facts that the respondent was the warden for 15 months, that he was the most senior figure and so forth. It's clearly a substantial role, one that kept the whole enterprise running. We would submit that the contribution need not be a sine qua non of the joint criminal enterprise. To give the analogy of the murder committed by a group of perpetrators, presumably the most important contributor of the sine qua non is the person who commits the actual actus reus but that is not to say that others aren't liable as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. In relation to the mens rea element, in response to a question by Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, my colleague for the Defence said that the Prosecution had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the respondent knew of the intent of the perpetrators. Again, I would refer to my submissions in chief. I cited paragraph 127, again of the trial judgement, in which the Trial Chamber found in relation to the imprisonment that the respondent knew of his contribution to the maintenance of the unlawful system by the principal offenders. So we have a finding of fact by the Trial Chamber. And paragraph 171, in relation to the inhumane conditions, where the Trial Chamber said that it was satisfied that the accused was aware of the intent of the principal offenders. I would submit, therefore, that we have findings of fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: If my colleague for the Defence is alleging that no reasonable trier of fact could have come to that conclusion, that is the standard to be met, we submit it has not been met. The last issue was whether the respondent, if he knew of the intent, shared that intent. Again, the Defence says that the Prosecution hasn't proved that. Our submission was that the error of the Trial Chamber was to look for an express agreement in each case for the commission of a crime by the joint criminal enterprise, and in fact the approach of the Trial Chamber in that respect was very similar to the way that it looked for some kind of express statement every time a beating was committed to see if that was committed on a discriminatory purpose. In a way, the Trial Chamber was always looking for direct evidence that went inside the subjective mind of the perpetrator at the relevant time. And our submission, as I said, is that it's normally rare, particularly in the kind of cases that come before this Tribunal, that one has direct evidence of a state of mind and that normally intent is inferred from surrounding circumstances. Again, I won't repeat the body of my main submissions, but we have findings of fact by the Trial Chamber that the respondent was in the position of warden. It was accepted voluntarily. He was the most senior figure. He was there for 15 months with knowledge of the systematic crimes being committed there. I have submitted that intent is different to motive, and the only reasonable conclusion on the facts as found was that intent existed. Now, I've set out the Prosecution's submissions on what the test for intent is. I referred in that respect to Article 30 of the Statute of the International Criminal Court. My colleague for the Defence has adopted a slightly different test in his submissions. He used expressions such as "the will to carry out," "prepared to accept as his own," and "volition to that effect." Now, I note the test for intent may vary from legal system to legal system. Precisely because of that the Tadic appeal judgement said at paragraph 225 that solutions to legal issues of this kind are not to be found in national legal systems. But I would simply make the observation that the kind of language being used by my colleague for the Defence is rather reminiscent for the test for intent distinguishing between a principal and aider and abettor under German law. This was a test referred to in the Stakic case in a decision on a rule 98 bis motion for judgement of acquittal of the 31st of October, 2002, at paragraph 58 and if I could quote if briefly there it said: "Under German law, the perpetrator has to have the animus auctoris, the additional intent to act as perpetrator. The animus auctoris reflecting the intent of the direct perpetrator requires an active will to commit the offence. The animus socii, by contrast, reflects the intent of an aider and abettor of the offence." Now, as I say, I'm not an expert on German law, but my understanding is that even in Germany in the 1950s and 1960s, I believe the German courts did look for evidence of a purely subjective state of mind. But more recently from the 1970s even under German law this animus auctoris is determined by the courts by reference to surrounding circumstances and objective factors such as that, and we submit that this is an approach simply of common sense, that in crimes of the kind the Tribunal deals with on a very large scale, direct evidence of a perpetrator's state of mind will be very rare. It will almost inevitably be inferred from all of the surrounding circumstances and that if any other approach were adopted, almost anyone involved in large scale crimes against international humanitarian law would be an aider and abettor and not a perpetrator. Turning then to the Prosecution's second ground of appeal. Mention was made of the principle that the Prosecution asserts a flexibility in drafting indictments. I think that's simply a fact that the Tribunal as a legal system has not developed to the point where there is a very rigid requirement for the way indictments are drafted. The desirability of developments in this effect is not denied, but at this stage there has been a flexibility in practice and acknowledgement in case law that there are no rigid requirements. The obligation to give notice to the Defence of the nature of the case again the accused is acknowledged. Our point was that the indictment, though, need not plead law and need not plead evidence. The question is whether by omitting specific reference to a legal theory in the indictment that that legal theory cannot be relied upon. It was also suggested that if the extended form of joint criminal enterprise is not expressly referred to in the indictment, that this would lead to the result that an accused might be convicted on something he had not been charged with in the indictment. That's certainly not the Prosecution contention. Our starting point was the assumption that an indictment contains general language that certainly would include the extended form of joint criminal enterprise. If the language of the whole of Article 7(1) is pleaded in an indictment, then as a matter of logic, all forms of participation under Article 7(1) are included, including joint criminal enterprise liability and including the extended form. So, it's not a case of including something in the judgement of a Trial Chamber that wasn't pleaded. On the contrary, to exclude the extended form of joint criminal enterprise liability would be to ignore something that in fact is contained in the indictment. It is our submission that a Trial Chamber needs to consider all modes of liability that are pleaded in the indictment. The question is not whether it's in the indictment or not, the question is whether greater detail needs to be given to the Defence. And as we say, that's a matter of fact in all the circumstances and that if the Defence has any difficulties in that respect, as I made the point in my main submissions, that needs to be raised by the Defence at the appropriate time. That concludes my reply on the second ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would the Defence ask for particulars?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The Defence might ask for particulars. There is a variety of remedies including pre-trial briefs, anything else. But, of course, normally this is resolved at the pre-trial stage. I would ask the Trial Chamber to call on my colleague Ms. Brady to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in reply I can be extremely brief. There are two points I wish to reply to in relation to torture and one point in relation to persecution. Your Honours, in relation to torture, Mr. Bakrac has submitted that basically the information wasn't enough to put him -- to be alarming information putting him on inquiry notice or giving him reason to know about the tortures. And basically what he's done is to break down the evidence, to parse the evidence, the major strands of evidence that we relied on as his reason to know. And in our submission, really this is not an appropriate way of proceeding. Our submission is based on a package of knowledge, and the package of knowledge includes the knowledge of what he was told by the witness RJ. It includes what he knows from what he saw happen to Ekrem Zekovic, and it includes his knowledge of having seen the widespread marks on detainees walking around or perhaps not walking around because they were so injured but limping around. And indeed that package has to be examined in light of the discriminatory nature of the inhumane conditions and the living conditions and the imprisonment of the detainees. And it's our submission that if this is not enough to trigger the duty to inquire then what is. I won't go through each and every one of those indicia, as it were, that should have alerted him to the torture but I would like to say in response he seemed to be submitting as a legal principle that the superior has to know about the -- has to have information as to the exact nature of the crime, that the information itself has to somehow have the -- contain the information. And this, in our submission, is simply not correct as a matter of law, and indeed in the Celebici case, it was held that the information available to the superior does not have to be information as to the exact nature of a crime. It's enough -- it has to be enough to put the superior on notice. It doesn't actually have to say,"There's torture going on out there, and it's on this prohibited purpose." It has to be enough to place him on notice that he's got to do something further. I also would like to respond to the second point on torture, and that is when he said that there would be no certainty or there would be no certainty that any investigation would have disclosed that torture was happening as a conclusive fact. And I think that this shows a misunderstanding of what 7(3) liability is all about, and it's about a derelict -- a culpability for a dereliction of duty for not even doing the investigation. It's not so much premised on an assumption on what might have been the final outcome, what might have been discovered had he done the investigation, because indeed he doesn't even have to complete the investigation - perhaps he takes steps to start it and to send the necessary reports on - but rather it's about his dereliction of duty in not investigating when he had notice or information that clearly placed him on inquiry notice that the crimes were going on. That's all I'll say on torture. I'll turn to address one point raised by Mr. Bakrac in relation to persecution based on beatings. And the main thrust of his argument was that basically by the Prosecution arguing for a contextual approach to the assessment of discriminatory intent, we've somehow -- the Prosecution is trying to shift or evade its burden of proof.
