Your Honours, the Prosecution is certainly not seeking to shift the burden of proof which remains firmly on the Prosecution. We are not doing that. But in reality, most cases -- in most cases, the only way you can prove intent for a crime - and this is both in the Tribunal cases and we know from national cases - the only way to prove it is to infer it from all the surrounding circumstances. It's extremely rare to have a case -- or not rare but it's not as common to have a case where there's a direct expression of the intent, that the actual perpetrator yells out his intent at the same time as doing the act, or even that makes it -- it's not a given that the person would have made a confession which would have revealed his intention at the time. One must be able to -- and the Trial Chamber must be able to infer intent from surrounding circumstances, especially -- and here the circumstances are the systemic nature of discriminatory conduct in the KP Dom and the systematic nature of the beatings therein. And to -- this context was comprised of frequency and a repetitive pattern of beatings which in fact makes it highly unlikely that it could have been motivated by completely extraneous factors. Our submission is that the -- if the evidence discloses a widespread pattern of acts which have taken place in an environment that is overwhelmingly marked by discrimination on one of the listed grounds - racial, religious, or political grounds - the only rational inference in the absence of any evidence to the contrary is that these acts were in the significant part carried out with the requisite discriminatory intent. In other words, we're saying that the inference is compelled when this sort of environment which is overwhelmingly marked by discrimination exists. And in particular, we point out the close proximity, that is a major feature of the acts, the beatings, in time and place to the other crimes which were found indisputably to have been committed on discriminatory grounds, and by the same people we're talking about, the guards, the same ones. This doesn't reverse the burden of proof. It's still clearly on the Prosecution to adduce the evidence, the high level of evidence to trigger that presumption. So what we're saying in summary is that if the Trial Chamber can conclude that yes, these acts took place, and yes, this is an environment overwhelmingly marked by systematically discriminatory practices, the Prosecution has difficulty -- or asks rhetorically, why should an accused hide behind a hypothetical -- possible hypothetical example in that sort of situation? And the drawing of permissible evidentiary presumptions is recognised in a number of jurisdictions. We've put them in our brief, coming from both civil law and common law case law and from the regional human rights decisions. For example, from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and I think Your Honours will find those authorities extremely helpful in your thinking on this. And even, indeed, this Tribunal has recognised legitimate presumptions being drawn in certain situations, and I won't go into detail on this to allow my colleagues to have time to reply on their grounds, but I draw Your Honours' attention to the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber, paragraph 42. And even indeed Your Honours' decision in the Kunarac Appeals Chamber decision on rape, that where there was evidence of force and threat of force and coercion, in the absence of no other evidence, there is no other possibility; there can be no consent. And it's a similar type of analysis here. Those are my submissions in reply, and if I cannot be of any further assistance, I will call on my colleague Ms. Norul Rashid to reply on the sixth and seventh grounds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I wish to respond to two points which my learned friend has raised. They both -- they both relate to deportation, the seventh ground. Learned counsel has raised the issue of deportation or, rather, transfer. He gave an example of a transfer of Muslims from their homes to KP Dom. This is similar to the question that you, I think, two of the learned Judges have raised, Judge Shahabuddeen and Judge Schomburg, which unfortunately, I think I did not respond to. I will take this opportunity to respond to Your Honours' queries. Your Honours, the position with regard to house-to-house transfer or what I perceive to be short-distance transfer is simply this: The act of deportation as defined, for instance in the Blaskic Trial Chamber or under Article 7(1)(D) of the ICC Statute, place no limits. Distance is not an issue here. And as I've elaborated in my submissions earlier, the focus is on the interests that deportation seeks to protect and the harm that it seeks to prevent. The very essence of the act of deportation is the unlawful or forcible displacement of an individual from their places of residences. The answer, the short answer to the question raised by counsel and Your Honours is yes. It also depends on why the victim was transferred, and yes, the Prosecution consider that it does have the responsibility to show that the deportation was unlawful under international law. So it all depends on whether all the elements of deportation, Your Honour, are satisfied on the facts of the case. If the victim was forcibly removed from one house and transferred to another house for security reasons or imperative military reasons as provided for in Geneva law, then that might not amount to deportation. On the facts of this case, no such exceptions arose on the facts of this case. It was never alleged, and there was just no evidence that the victims or the detainees were transferred for security or military reasons. The fact that the detainees were removed from their homes to KP Dom, theoretically speaking, that is deportation. They have been removed, forcibly removed from their homes. That, of course, was not the allegation, I'm just responding to my learned friend's hypothetical situation. Most of the detainees who left KP Dom who were so-called exchanged or transferred out of KP Dom simply disappeared. This sort of situation is not uncommon in conflicts. In the case of Srebrenica, we're talking about 25.000 women and children who were deported from one place to another. If forces -- if the Serb forces walk into Ahmici and decided to expel all the Muslim inhabitants, expel them not really concerned as to where they ended up but with the sole objective of making sure that they leave Ahmici, it is virtually impossible for the Prosecution to prove where each and every of these detainees ended up, or, rather, the victim ended up. Some of them may end up as refugees still living within the region. Some of them ended up in Germany, in Holland. We don't know. This is the reason why we submit that the focus of the act of deportation has to be on the act of removal and not the final destination. The second point that counsel has raised is in relation to the exchange, and here, Your Honour, I wish to clarify my earlier responses in relation to the exchange. It is unclear in international law as to whether exchanges as such are crimes. It is simply not clear, and we have not briefed the Appeals Chamber in our appeal brief specifically on this issue simply because the issue did not arise on the facts. So the issue of legality of exchanges or otherwise is still unclear. The Trial Chamber categorised the deportation incidents as so-called exchanges on the facts because, as we allege in the indictment, they were in fact acts of transfers. The Defence at trial did not allege that the exchanges, the so-called exchanges that occurred were legal. The Defence -- the defence at trial was that Krnojelac was not responsible for the exchange programme, that it was someone else, Marko Kovac, a military person who was responsible for these activities. That was his defence. The issue of the legality of the exchanges, it was never litigated and it was not in fact an issue at trial. If the Appeals Chamber wishes us to review further on this matter we would be more than happy to assist. We could file further briefs on this issue, but on the facts of this case, Your Honour, and for purposes of this appeal, it is simply not relevant. That concludes my reply, Your Honour. I believe my learned colleague Mr. Carmona wishes to address the Court on the final two grounds, grounds number four and eight. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Rashid. Mr. Carmona. You really have no luck today. You're always last.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honours, I just wish initially to raise a particular point that was raised by one of your learned personnel in relation to paragraph 98. What in fact -- concerns were raised -- sorry. Concerns were raised about whether, for example, a certificate that in fact was brought before the Court that was dated the 11th of January, 2000, whether in fact the Defence was allowed to submit this document for evaluation by the Trial Chamber. But one needs to look at the history of that particular procedure that took place, because what in fact happened is that there was another document that was in fact dated from -- the other document was Momcilo Mandzic, the president, who in fact had appointed -- had appointed Krnojelac in a permanent capacity as warden effective from the 17th of May, 1992. And what had happened is that basically that document came of course from the Department of Justice. The document was -- that the Defence was seeking to tender was a document from the Department of Defence, and that document was -- represented a summary of data in relation to the rule and function and responsibilities of, in fact, Krnojelac to the extent that in fact it said essentially that his responsibility was really in terms of seeing about property at KP Dom. The Court, the Trial Chamber, out of an abundance of caution recognised that there were two contentious documents, asked the Defence, "Listen. You said this was in fact a summary of data. Is that data contemporaneous? Because in fact we have here a document that is contemporaneous and it can affect the weight that will attach this particular document." Of course they left with them the option of getting additional material and of course tendering the document if they so desired, and they didn't. So the extent to the fact that they didn't tender of the document, it appears that there was some kind of waiver in that area. Apart from that, even the Prosecution attempted to cross-examine on that document that was not in fact in evidence and it was objected to by the Defence. So it is really an inconsistent approach to hint that maybe in fact they weren't given the opportunity to tender this particular document in evidence when in fact that particular facility was available and they never exercised it. But again, it is not something that I don't want to go in contentiously because I suspect my friend will continue to raise that document tomorrow and I will have to respond to it factually. Apart from that, my learned friend indicated that in terms of the evidence that one could not really come to the conclusion that in fact the killings did in fact occur. Again my learned colleague, Ms. Brady, has in fact indicated that as much as in fact, for example, there is no need for specific knowledge, I will add to that that there is in fact no need to be aware of all the elements of the offence. You know, this is what Celebici, in fact, says. In relation to RJ, I am a bit nonplussed by the response of my learned colleague in relation to RJ when he says that the Defence considers that what the witness said to the accused was not necessarily true. But this particular witness was a confidant in fact of Krnojelac, (redacted) and in fact was very supportive of his position because they indicated -- he indicated very matter-of-factly when he was arrested he said, "No, not Mico. Mico couldn't have been arrested," you know. But of course in fact he was. So the evidence that RJ gave in relation and -- in relation to his conversations with in fact the Krnojelac is something that in fact that I think the Court believed and specifically in terms of bringing knowledge to the appellant in regard to what was happening, there is line 'T' at page T3867 when, for example, when he told Krnojelac about the large group of people missing, Krnojelac's response was, "(redacted) you just don't ask anything. Don't ask me. I don't know." You know. Okay. The other point that my friend raised was the question of whether there was a need for retroactive investigation in relation to the particular incident involving Ekrem Zekovic. You will recall that in fact that particular beating took place sometime about the 8th of 9th of July, some three weeks before, in fact, Krnojelac demoted office, and he's saying that Krnojelac, that particular incident couldn't have been used by us to illustrate in fact that it would have put him on inquiry notice. But the bottom line is this, is that it concerned an individual who in fact everyone agreed, it was common knowledge, was a man of extremely violent temperament during the conflict, before the conflict. One individual, in an objective view, ought not to have been a guard in the camp given his general deportment. So that as much as, in fact, for example it was late in the day, it did not in fact preempt him from his responsibility to inquire further. And there is no evidence that in fact he did in relation to this particular incident and there is no evidence in relation to any particular incident involving Burilo he in fact checked out. Which in fact he would have been entitled to by virtue of that startling information that came to his attention and what he saw, because he was there when that beating was taking place. With regard to the absence from the camp, I think in fact this is -- this is adequately responded to by our -- in our -- in our brief at footnote 184. We make reference to the ICRC commentary to the Additional Protocol at page 1014 where we say for example that the fact the respondent was absent for a period of seven days is in and of itself immaterial to the respondent's superior liability because "a superior cannot absolve himself from responsibility by pleading ignorance of reports addressed to him or by invoking temporary absence as an excuse." And you would recall only that in fact in Mucic in Celebici, his in fact was a similar type complaint although it found no favour with the Appeals Chamber with regard to his absenting himself a lot from the camp. Granted, of course, he was there for only seven months as opposed to in fact Krnojelac who was there for some 15 months. With regard to my friend's concern that I raised the issue of the position of the warden, it was raised in the context of his conformist personality and the fact that the Trial Chamber had in fact used that as a basis for placing less weight on his superior responsibility. And we were contending that someone who in fact voluntarily accepts a post in those circumstances cannot know in fact -- and one who is a commander in the scheme of things, cannot know, in fact indicate, "Well, listen, my position as a warden is something that in fact would not have been considered." In relation to the whole issue with regard to victims, again we have in fact in our brief adequately responded in our response with regard to the expanding rule of the definition of victim, internationally and also related to the extent that FWS-183 had indicated -- and if I may in fact refer particularly to -- FWS-183 did in fact refer to -- to the type of -- I do have my document here. Sorry about that. Yes. Yes. FWS-183 did in fact indicate and gave evidence with regard to the type of hurt and pain endured by families in terms of lack of visits, in terms of a daughter in fact knowing her father's out there being beaten, things like that. So again in fact that has been responded to in our brief. With regard to the issue of cooperation, we do not think, for example, that the pliancy of counsel is a factor they needs to be considered in the area of sentence. At the end of the day it is all about conduct. Again, we have indicated in our response, in our reply to the response why it is, for example, we think so, that counsel in this Tribunal has certain responsibilities that are in fact -- ought not to fall under the umbrella of the unity of counsel and client, that in fact the fact that counsel helps to expedite matters has nothing to do with the conduct of the accused or the appellant at the time in question. And then fourthly, with regard to the whole issue of a comparison with regard to other individuals who are in fact of similar ilk in the context of the position they held in the camp and in the context of the sentencing that they received, it is important to know that both Celebici and Kupreskic were quite adamant that any kind of analysis being done with regard to using the precedents, if I may so call it, in terms of sentencing must be on the basis of substantial similarity, not general similarity. And in this regard, for example, we need to consider certain peculiarities about Aleksovski, for example, who in fact the Court said very categorically would have in fact attracted a far weightier sentence than he did only because of issues of double jeopardy and the fact that he was facing the court on two occasions. The bottom line is in fact we are also in fact saying that in the event that the learned Appeals Chamber finds favour with our arguments with regard to the offences in terms of the killings, in terms of torture, that certainly in fact you are talking about killings involving some 26 individuals, or in fact 23, that it is -- it is a factor that in fact would loom large in considering whether, for example, the sentence in fact meets the appropriate standard. And I say this more so when one considers, for example, the -- and if I may in fact end up -- if I may consider what in fact the Trial Chamber indicated at paragraph 514, that the sentence in this case must make it clear to others who, like the accused, seek to avoid the responsibilities of command which accompany the position which they have accepted, that their failure to carry out these responsibilities will still be punished. If you are prepared, in other words, to take the benefit, you must take the burden. And I dare say it is puzzling. Our sentence of seven and a half years can effectively transmit what I would refer to as the hallowed objectives of the said Trial Chamber. Without more, I think this is in fact the end of my submissions in terms of responding to my -- the concerns of my learned friend on the other side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Carmona. I don't think there are any questions. No. All right. We're going to suspend the hearing and say that we'll see one another tomorrow at 9.00 for the Defence appeal. Let's try not to repeat ourselves. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.42 p.m.,
